hemorrhoids-guide.question: How do you treat hemorrhoids?
hemorrhoids-guide.answerHtml: Hemorrhoids are treated stepwise. Most people can start at home with a high-fiber diet (NIDDK cites 28 g daily on a 2,000-calorie diet), water and other nonalcoholic liquids, warm sitz baths, and not straining or sitting on the toilet for long. The ASCRS guidelines, as summarized in American Family Physician, strongly recommend increasing fiber and fluid intake. For short-term relief, over-the-counter options such as witch hazel pads (up to 6 times daily) or hydrocortisone 1% (no more than 3 to 4 times daily) can help, but the NIDDK notes that doctors most often recommend over-the-counter products for 1 week and advises seeing a doctor if symptoms last beyond 1 week or you have rectal bleeding. Hemorrhoids that persist despite home care can be treated with office procedures, and a meta-analysis of randomized trials recommends rubber band ligation as the first procedure for grade 1 to 3 hemorrhoids, reserving hemorrhoidectomy for hemorrhoids that do not respond. Rectal bleeding warrants evaluation, since it can also be a sign of Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or colorectal cancer. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can evaluate symptoms and recommend the appropriate treatment.

acid-reflux-gerd-guide.question: How do you treat acid reflux (GERD)?
acid-reflux-gerd-guide.answerHtml: Population studies put GERD prevalence in North America at 18.1% to 27.8% (El-Serag et al., Gut). The 2022 ACG Clinical Guideline recommends an 8-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) once daily before a meal for classic heartburn and regurgitation without alarm symptoms, with the PPI taken 30 to 60 minutes before the meal, and an attempt to stop or switch to on-demand use once symptoms respond. FDA labeling lists omeprazole 20 mg once daily for up to 4 weeks for symptomatic GERD (Prilosec label). The ACG recommends PPIs over H2 blockers such as famotidine for healing erosive esophagitis. It also recommends weight loss for people who are overweight and suggests avoiding meals within 2 to 3 hours of bedtime and raising the head of the bed for nighttime symptoms. Dysphagia or other alarm symptoms such as weight loss or GI bleeding call for endoscopy first. A licensed clinician, by telehealth or in person, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

acne-treatment-guide.question: What is the most effective treatment for acne?
acne-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Per the 2024 AAD acne guideline, combining topical therapies with multiple mechanisms of action is a good practice statement, and strong recommendations are made for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, and oral doxycycline. The guideline also lists limiting systemic antibiotic use, and combining systemic antibiotics with topical therapies, as good practice. Spironolactone and combined oral contraceptive pills receive conditional recommendations. Oral isotretinoin is strongly recommended for acne that is severe, causing psychosocial burden or scarring, or failing standard oral or topical therapy. Acne affects nearly 50 million Americans each year. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

ai-chatbot-medical-information-safety.question: Is it safe to use AI chatbots like ChatGPT for medical information?
ai-chatbot-medical-information-safety.answerHtml: AI chatbots can help with general health education, but they carry documented risks. In a Pew Research Center survey conducted in October 2025, 22% of U.S. adults said they get health information from AI chatbots at least sometimes, and only 18% of those users rated it highly accurate. A 2026 BMJ Open audit of the free versions of five chatbots, prompted on February 1, 2025 with deliberately challenging questions, rated 49.6% of 250 responses problematic. In a 2026 randomized study in Nature Medicine, the models alone identified the relevant condition in 94.9% of cases, but people using them did so in fewer than 34.5%, no better than a control group. In a 2026 Nature Medicine test, ChatGPT Health under-triaged 52% of emergency cases. Safe use rules: never rely on a chatbot to decide whether a symptom needs emergency care, and confirm diagnoses or drug decisions with a licensed clinician.

ai-chatbots-vs-physicians-diagnostic-acc.question: How accurate are AI chatbots compared to physicians at diagnosing medical conditions?
ai-chatbots-vs-physicians-diagnostic-acc.answerHtml: A 2025 npj Digital Medicine meta-analysis of 83 studies published from June 2018 to June 2024, mostly testing GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, found an overall generative AI diagnostic accuracy of 52.1%; AI did not differ significantly from physicians overall or from non-expert physicians, but trailed expert physicians by 15.8 percentage points. In a 2026 Oxford randomized study in Nature Medicine, 1,298 UK adults using GPT-4o, Llama 3 or Command R+ on ten written medical scenarios chose the right course of action no more often than a control group using their usual sources, such as internet search, and identified relevant conditions less often. ECRI reported chatbots inventing body parts and wrongly approving an electrosurgical electrode placement that could cause burns. A licensed clinician, reached by telehealth or an in-person visit, provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

ai-respiratory-symptom-triage.question: Can AI chatbots safely triage respiratory symptoms like shortness of breath or cough?
ai-respiratory-symptom-triage.answerHtml: Current evidence does not show that AI chatbots can safely triage breathing problems on their own. In a 2026 Nature Medicine study from Mount Sinai that tested ChatGPT Health in January 2026 (960 responses to 60 clinician-written vignettes), 52% of responses to gold-standard emergencies were under-triaged to a 24 to 48 hour doctor visit instead of the emergency department, including impending respiratory failure in asthma. When friends or family were quoted minimizing symptoms, triage recommendations shifted more often in edge cases (odds ratio 11.7), with most shifts toward less urgent care. In a 2025 test of ChatGPT models on emergency department cases, nearly all models missed pneumonia when the notes said the patient had no fever. A 2026 JMIR viewpoint noted that AI triage evidence comes mostly from retrospective validations, emergency settings, or vignettes, with scant evaluation of real-world outcomes. A licensed clinician, reached via telehealth or an in-person visit, provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

altitude-sickness-diamox-guide.question: How does Diamox (acetazolamide) prevent altitude sickness?
altitude-sickness-diamox-guide.answerHtml: Acetazolamide (Diamox) is the only FDA-approved pharmacological prophylaxis for acute mountain sickness (AMS). It works as a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: blocking the enzyme in the kidneys causes bicarbonate excretion and a mild metabolic acidosis, which stimulates the respiratory center to increase ventilation rate and depth, elevating arterial oxygen saturation and accelerating acclimatization. Per the CDC Yellow Book, the recommended prophylaxis dose is 125 mg twice daily starting 24 hours before ascent, continued for 2 days at maximum altitude. The Wilderness Medical Society guidelines confirm 125 mg BID equals the older 250 mg BID dose in efficacy with fewer side effects. Acetazolamide is contraindicated with sulfa allergy and in all trimesters of pregnancy.

anti-aging-treatment-guide.question: What anti-aging skin treatments actually work?
anti-aging-treatment-guide.answerHtml: The strongest evidence-based anti-aging interventions are daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen and prescription tretinoin. UV exposure drives 80–90% of visible skin aging; the American Academy of Dermatology recommends SPF 30+ applied daily year-round. A systematic review of seven RCTs, which tested concentrations from 0.025% to 5%, found topical tretinoin consistently improves wrinkling, hyperpigmentation, and lentigines, with benefit as early as one month and maintained at 24 months. Common prescription cream strengths are 0.025% to 0.1%. OTC retinol is ~10× weaker and slower. Vitamin C serum (L-ascorbic acid 10–20%) adds antioxidant protection. Procedures (chemical peels, lasers) address Grade III–IV photoaging and require in-person dermatology. Tretinoin and retinoids are contraindicated in pregnancy. A licensed clinician (accessible via telehealth or in-person care) can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

anxiety-depression-medication-guide.question: What medications are used to treat anxiety and depression?
anxiety-depression-medication-guide.answerHtml: About 19.1% of U.S. adults had an anxiety disorder in the past year, and an estimated 21.0 million (8.3%) had a major depressive episode in 2021, per NIMH statistics on anxiety and depression. For adults with depression, the APA clinical practice guideline recommends either psychotherapy or a second-generation antidepressant, and NICE NG222 (last reviewed January 2026) says SSRIs should be considered the first choice for most people. For generalized anxiety disorder, NICE CG113 recommends an SSRI first, then another SSRI or an SNRI. FDA labels list an adult starting dose of 50 mg a day and a maximum of 200 mg a day for sertraline in depression, and 10 mg once daily (maximum 20 mg) for escitalopram in depression or GAD. NICE says that if an antidepressant is going to work, an effect is usually seen within 4 weeks. Do not stop an antidepressant abruptly: FDA labels advise reducing the dose gradually, and NICE advises tapering in stages, which may take weeks or months. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in person, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

asthma-guide.question: How is asthma treated according to the latest guidelines?
asthma-guide.answerHtml: Nearly 28 million people in the U.S. have asthma, and nearly all asthma deaths are avoidable with the right treatment and care, per the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. The GINA 2025 summary guide says adults and adolescents with asthma should not be treated with a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA, such as albuterol) alone, and that treatment should include an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS). Low-dose ICS-formoterol is the preferred reliever for adolescents and adults; used as needed, it reduces emergency visits or hospitalizations by 65% compared with SABA alone. Maintenance-and-reliever therapy (SMART) uses one ICS-formoterol inhaler both daily and as needed; in trials reviewed for the NAEPP 2020 Focused Updates, it reduced exacerbations by 32% compared with the same-dose ICS-LABA plus a SABA reliever in people 12 and older. Severe attack signs include talking in single words, sitting hunched forward, and peak flow at or below 50% of best; drowsiness, confusion or a silent chest are life-threatening. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

at-home-uti-test-guide.question: Are at-home UTI test strips accurate, and when should I trust the result?
at-home-uti-test-guide.answerHtml: At-home UTI dipsticks measure two chemical signals, nitrite and leukocyte esterase. In a 70-study meta-analysis (Devillé 2004), sensitivity when at least one pad was positive ranged from 68 to 88% across patient groups, and positive results still needed confirmation. In a primary care study of 434 women (Little 2010), a dipstick rule was 75% sensitive and 66% specific. A negative strip does not reliably rule out UTI when symptoms are present. Performance falls further in older adults; a 2026 meta-analysis found dipstick specificity of only 39% for predicting UTI in symptomatic adults aged 60 and older. The 2026 EAU guideline gives dipstick testing only a weak recommendation for diagnosing acute cystitis and says to diagnose recurrent cystitis by urine culture. Skip the strip entirely if you have red flags (fever, flank pain, visible blood, pregnancy, symptoms >7 days, or new symptoms in a man). For everyone else, contact a licensed clinician for evaluation. A telehealth visit is often the fastest evidence-based path to a treatment decision.

atencion-medica-para-visitantes-de-mexic.question: ¿Cómo puede un visitante desde México mantener sus recetas y condiciones crónicas en orden durante un viaje a EE.UU.?
atencion-medica-para-visitantes-de-mexic.answerHtml: En 2024, 13.4 millones de mexicanos visitaron EE.UU. por tierra (NTTO 2024). La ley federal exige que una farmacia estadounidense surta los medicamentos de receta con la receta de un profesional autorizado por la ley (21 U.S.C. 353(b)), por lo que, en general, una receta mexicana no puede surtirse en EE.UU.; una consulta con un médico con licencia en EE.UU., incluida la telesalud, puede resultar en una receta para medicamentos crónicos no controlados (presión arterial, tiroides, diabetes oral, estatinas, la mayoría de inhaladores) si el médico lo considera apropiado. Bajo la Política de Importación Personal de la FDA, los extranjeros pueden traer o enviar un suministro de 90 días de medicamentos, y la FDA indica que un medicamento aprobado en otro país pero no aprobado en EE.UU. es ilegal de importar. Algunos medicamentos comúnmente recetados en México son sustancias controladas de la Lista IV en EE.UU. (Rivotril / clonazepam, Tafil / alprazolam, Ambien / zolpidem, tramadol), y la DEA permite a los visitantes extranjeros traer hasta 50 unidades de dosis de sustancias controladas para uso personal (DEA). Según el Reporte Nacional de Estadísticas de Diabetes de los CDC, la prevalencia cruda de diabetes diagnosticada en adultos mexicanos o mexicano-americanos fue del 11.1% (2019-2021), frente a 13.3% en adultos puertorriqueños y 8.5% en adultos blancos no hispanos. Las entidades cubiertas por la Sección 1557 de la Ley del Cuidado de Salud Asequible, como los hospitales que reciben asistencia financiera federal, deben proporcionar asistencia lingüística gratuita, incluidos intérpretes calificados (HHS OCR, carta de diciembre de 2024; implementación plena antes del 5 de julio de 2025).

azo-home-uti-test-strips-review.question: What do pink, purple, positive, and negative AZO UTI test-strip results mean?
azo-home-uti-test-strips-review.answerHtml: Use the result pattern and symptoms together. A positive leukocyte pad means leukocyte esterase, an enzyme from white blood cells, was detected; a positive nitrite pad suggests bacteria that convert nitrate to nitrite. Positive leukocytes with negative nitrites can reflect a UTI caused by an organism that does not make nitrite, urine that was not held in the bladder long enough, contamination, or another cause of white blood cells in the urine. A negative strip does not reliably rule out UTI when burning, urgency, or frequency continues. AZO’s current directions say to read the nitrite pad at 1 minute and the leukocyte pad at 2 minutes, and to ignore any color change after 3 minutes. In the Devillé meta-analysis, leukocyte esterase alone had sensitivity of 48 to 86% and nitrite alone 45 to 60%. Seek clinical assessment for persistent symptoms; fever, flank pain, vomiting, pregnancy, recurrent symptoms, or urinary symptoms in a man call for medical care rather than reliance on a home test.

bacterial-vaginosis-bv-guide.question: What is the best treatment for bacterial vaginosis in 2026?
bacterial-vaginosis-bv-guide.answerHtml: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a common vaginal condition: a U.S. national survey found BV in about 29 percent of women aged 14 to 49, or about 21 million women, and 84 percent of women with BV reported no symptoms. The 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines recommend three regimens for women with symptoms: metronidazole 500 mg by mouth twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel once daily for 5 days, or clindamycin 2% cream at bedtime for 7 days. A single 2 g dose of secnidazole oral granules is a CDC alternative regimen; in a phase 3 trial cited by CDC, clinical cure at days 21 to 30 was 53 percent with secnidazole versus 19 percent with placebo. The harder clinical problem is recurrence: 58 percent of women had BV return within 12 months after oral metronidazole in a cohort study by Bradshaw and colleagues. For women with repeated episodes, twice-weekly metronidazole gel lowered recurrence during 16 weeks of suppression to 25.5 percent versus 59.1 percent on placebo, and in a 2025 New England Journal of Medicine trial of women in monogamous relationships, also treating the male partner lowered 12-week recurrence to 35 percent versus 63 percent with treatment of the woman alone. The 2021 CDC guideline predates that trial and does not recommend routine partner treatment. A licensed clinician can confirm the diagnosis with testing and tailor a treatment and suppression plan to each person.

birth-control-refills-guide.question: Do you need a doctor's visit to refill hormonal birth control?
birth-control-refills-guide.answerHtml: No routine exam is usually required. CDC's 2024 U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations say blood pressure should be measured before starting combined pills, patch or ring and that a pelvic examination is not necessary; among healthy patients, no examinations or tests are needed before progestin-only pills. CDC recommends providing up to a 1-year supply (for example, 13 pill packs) and notes that restricting the number of pill packs can be a barrier and might increase risk for pregnancy. Call a clinician or go to an emergency room right away for leg pain that will not go away, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a sudden change in vision, or a sudden, severe headache unlike your usual headaches (FDA patient labeling). A licensed clinician, by telehealth or in person, can review your history and decide whether a refill is appropriate.

cat-bite-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a cat bite?
cat-bite-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Wash the bite right away with soap and running water, then decide quickly whether it needs a physician. Cat bites tend to cause deep puncture wounds and are all considered high risk for infection (Ellis and Ellis, AFP 2014), and Pasteurella species were found in 75% of infected cat bites in a multicenter emergency department study (Talan et al., NEJM 1999). IDSA recommends 3 to 5 days of preemptive antibiotics for higher-risk bites, including moderate to severe injuries (especially the hand or face), swelling, possible joint or bone penetration, and people who are immunocompromised, asplenic or have advanced liver disease. Infected bites are treated with an antibiotic active against both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, such as amoxicillin-clavulanate (IDSA 2014), for which IDSA lists an adult dose of 875/125 mg twice daily (IDSA 2014 executive summary). Hand bites with swelling, redness or pain when moving a finger need in-person care the same day. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

cat-scratch-antibiotics-guide.question: Do you need antibiotics for a cat scratch?
cat-scratch-antibiotics-guide.answerHtml: Usually not. A shallow scratch washed promptly with soap and water typically heals on its own. A scratch that turns red, warm, swollen or pus-filled in the first few days is a skin infection, and for infected animal bites IDSA recommends an agent active against both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, such as amoxicillin-clavulanate (IDSA 2014). Cat scratch disease is different: tender lymph nodes 1 to 3 weeks after exposure, caused by Bartonella henselae (CDC). The CDC says it is usually self-limited, that antibiotics are sometimes recommended for otherwise healthy patients, and that they are required for immunocompromised patients. In one small randomized trial, azithromycin shrank nodes faster in the first 30 days, with no significant difference afterward (Bass et al., 1998). A swollen lymph node needs an in-person exam. Red streaks, fever with spreading redness, or a scratch over a finger joint with pain on movement need in-person care now.

cellulitis-guide.question: How is cellulitis treated?
cellulitis-guide.answerHtml: Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the deep dermis and the tissue just beneath it. The IDSA 2014 skin and soft tissue infection guideline recommends that typical cellulitis without systemic signs of infection be treated with an antibiotic active against streptococci, such as penicillin, cephalexin, dicloxacillin, or clindamycin, for 5 days, extended if the infection has not improved. When MRSA is a concern, oral options that cover both streptococci and MRSA include clindamycin alone, or TMP-SMX or doxycycline combined with a beta-lactam. The guideline recommends outpatient treatment for patients without SIRS (a body-wide inflammatory response), altered mental status, or unstable blood pressure, and hospitalization when a deeper or necrotizing infection is suspected or outpatient treatment is failing. In one hospital study, 30.5% of patients admitted from the emergency department for leg cellulitis were misdiagnosed, so getting the diagnosis right matters. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or an in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

chlamydia-treatment-guide.question: What is the CDC-recommended treatment for chlamydia in 2025?
chlamydia-treatment-guide.answerHtml: The CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines recommend doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days for adolescents and adults, with azithromycin 1 g as a single dose or levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 7 days as alternatives. In a randomized trial in men who have sex with men, microbiologic cure of rectal chlamydia was 100% with doxycycline versus 74% with azithromycin. CDC notes that chlamydia was found at the anorectal site in 33% to 83% of women with urogenital infection, regardless of reported anal sex. In pregnancy, azithromycin 1 g as a single dose is recommended, and doxycycline is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. The USPSTF recommends screening all sexually active women 24 and younger and older women at increased risk; CDC advises annual screening for sexually active women under 25. Abstain from sex for 7 days after single-dose therapy or until a 7-day course is finished, and until all partners have been treated. A licensed clinician, by telehealth or in person, can review symptoms and prescribe treatment.

cholesterol-hyperlipidemia-guide.question: What are the 2026 ACC/AHA guidelines for treating high cholesterol?
cholesterol-hyperlipidemia-guide.answerHtml: The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia, published March 13, 2026, retires and replaces the 2018 blood cholesterol guideline and covers the evaluation, management and monitoring of high blood cholesterol, hypertriglyceridemia and elevated lipoprotein(a). According to the American College of Cardiology's summary, it brings back LDL-C goals of <100 mg/dL for borderline or intermediate risk, <70 mg/dL for high risk, and <55 mg/dL for people with ASCVD at very high risk, uses the PREVENT-ASCVD equations instead of the Pooled Cohort Equations for adults aged 30 to 79, and says Lp(a) should be measured at least once in adulthood. Separately, the USPSTF (2022) recommends a statin for adults aged 40 to 75 with at least one cardiovascular risk factor and an estimated 10-year risk of 10% or greater. A 2026 Lancet meta-analysis of 19 double-blind statin trials (123,940 participants) found that, beyond known effects on muscle and diabetes, only 4 of 66 other label-listed side effects were linked to statins. The CDC reports that about 86 million U.S. adults have total cholesterol above 200 mg/dL. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

chronic-conditions-visiting-parents-guid.question: How can I keep my visiting parents' chronic conditions stable during a US trip?
chronic-conditions-visiting-parents-guid.answerHtml: For older international visitors with chronic conditions like hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, atrial fibrillation, COPD, or asthma, the four things that keep a US trip uneventful are a pre-travel visit with the home clinician at least 4 to 6 weeks before departure, a time-zone plan for daily medications agreed with that clinician, all prescriptions packed in original containers in carry-on luggage with a written medication list, and a low threshold to use US telehealth for a same-day check-in when something feels off. The CDC Yellow Book advises pre-travel consultation at least 4 to 6 weeks before departure and says travelers' chronic conditions should be controlled and managed optimally. For trips of about 5 time zones or fewer, or under 3 days, a practical review advises keeping watches on home time and taking basal insulin as usual; for 5 or more time zones with a stay longer than 3 days, it describes adjusting the basal insulin dose by about 4 percent per time zone crossed (westward travel leads to missed doses and eastward travel to excess doses, per Forst et al. 2021). In a randomized crossover trial, bedtime levothyroxine improved thyroid hormone levels compared with morning dosing (Bolk et al. 2010 Arch Intern Med), so bedtime dosing is an option to discuss with the prescriber for the trip. Evidence on melatonin for jet lag in older travelers is mixed: the CATMAT Statement on Older Travellers says it cannot be routinely recommended because of lack of evidence of benefit, while the CDC Yellow Book notes that 0.5 to 1 mg is often sufficient and that doses above 5 mg are not recommended.

cold-and-flu-guide.question: What does Tamiflu cost in 2026 and how do you get a prescription online?
cold-and-flu-guide.answerHtml: Tamiflu (generic oseltamivir) is FDA-approved to treat uncomplicated influenza in people who have had symptoms for no more than 48 hours, per the FDA-approved Tamiflu label, and the CDC clinicians summary notes that clinical benefit is greatest when treatment starts early, especially within 48 hours. The adult dose is 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, reduced when creatinine clearance is 60 mL/min or less. When checked on November 7, 2026, GoodRx listed generic oseltamivir 75 mg (10 capsules, one adult course) at $21.98 with its coupon versus a $57.26 retail price; prices vary by pharmacy. The 2014 systematic review by Jefferson and colleagues in the BMJ found oseltamivir shortened the time to first symptom relief in adults by about 16.8 hours, with no difference in hospital admissions in adult treatment trials. Xofluza (baloxavir) is a single-dose alternative; in the CAPSTONE-1 trial in NEJM, time to symptom relief was similar to oseltamivir, and the 2025 CENTERSTONE trial found it reduced laboratory-confirmed flu transmission to household contacts. Because the 48-hour window is tight, a same-day telehealth video visit with a physician is often the most practical way to get an e-prescription sent to a local pharmacy. A licensed clinician can screen for red flags, confirm eligibility, and e-prescribe oseltamivir by video visit where they are licensed.

cold-sores-hsv1-guide.question: What is the best treatment for a cold sore (HSV-1) in 2026?
cold-sores-hsv1-guide.answerHtml: Cold sores, also called fever blisters, are caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), which the World Health Organization estimates infected 64% of people under age 50 worldwide in 2020. The virus lives inside nerve cells and periodically reactivates to cause outbreaks on or around the lips. For an episodic outbreak, oral antivirals are the main option, and the FDA labels for valacyclovir (2 grams twice, 12 hours apart, for one day) and famciclovir (1,500 mg as a single dose) both call for starting at the earliest symptom, such as tingling. In placebo-controlled trials by Spruance and colleagues, one-day valacyclovir shortened the median episode by 1.0 day, and single-dose famciclovir shortened healing by about 2 days. Topical creams help less: docosanol 10% shortened healing by about 18 hours and penciclovir 1% by 0.7 day in their pivotal trials, and a review by Leung and Barankin rates oral antivirals superior to topical therapy for episodic treatment. Long-term daily oral antivirals reduce recurrences, though a Cochrane review judged the benefit small. A licensed clinician, accessible in person or through telehealth, can evaluate symptoms and prescribe oral antivirals when appropriate.

contact-dermatitis-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat contact dermatitis?
contact-dermatitis-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Contact dermatitis has two types: irritant (direct damage to the skin) and allergic (a delayed, T-cell mediated hypersensitivity). The AAD notes that only avoiding the cause gets rid of contact dermatitis. An American Family Physician review recommends mid- or high-potency topical steroids for localized allergic contact dermatitis and lower-potency steroids on thin skin such as the face and eyelids. For reactions covering more than 20 percent of the skin, the same review recommends oral prednisone for five to seven days, then a reduced dose for five to seven more days, and advises against steroid dose packs. Patch testing identifies the allergen when it remains unknown. Poison ivy, nickel, and fragrances are among the most common causes. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in person.

covid-19-paxlovid-treatment-guide.question: Who should consider Paxlovid within 5 days of COVID symptoms?
covid-19-paxlovid-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Paxlovid is a treatment option for adults at high risk of severe COVID-19, not an automatic prescription for every positive test. The current US label requires starting within 5 days of symptom onset and provides kidney-specific regimens, including severe impairment. Medicines must be checked for important interactions. IDSA guidance favors treatment for higher-risk adults, but newer vaccinated-patient trials did not demonstrate the original unvaccinated-trial benefit in every population. A clinician should weigh individual risk, current evidence, safety and access. Emergency warning signs require direct emergency care, not a routine online prescription.

d-mannose-uti-guide.question: Does D-mannose actually work for preventing UTIs?
d-mannose-uti-guide.answerHtml: In a large double-blind trial (Hayward 2024, N=598), 51.0% of women taking D-mannose and 55.7% taking placebo had another clinically suspected UTI, a difference that was not statistically significant, and the 2025 AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline amendment tells clinicians to inform patients that D-mannose alone "may not be effective" for UTI prevention. Better-supported options depend on the situation. For perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with recurrent UTIs, the guideline says clinicians should recommend vaginal estrogen (Moderate Recommendation), and a 2020 meta-analysis found vaginal estrogen lowered recurrent UTIs versus placebo (relative risk 0.42). Cranberry products reduced symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs (relative risk 0.74) in the 2023 Cochrane review. In the ALTAR trial (BMJ 2022), methenamine hippurate had 1.38 UTIs per person-year versus 0.89 with daily antibiotic prophylaxis; the difference stayed within the trial's non-inferiority margin, so methenamine was judged non-inferior. Women with recurrent UTIs who drink less than 1.5 L a day may be offered more water. Two newer oral antibiotics, pivmecillinam (Pivya, 2024) and gepotidacin (Blujepa, 2025), are approved for uncomplicated UTIs. Any of these can be discussed with a licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth.

dandruff-seborrheic-dermatitis-guide.question: What is the best dandruff shampoo, and how long should you leave it on?
dandruff-seborrheic-dermatitis-guide.answerHtml: There is no single best dandruff shampoo for every adult. Choose by active ingredient, scalp symptoms and the directions on the exact bottle. The AAD advises ingredient-based selection and hair-texture-aware use. The Nizoral 1% label directs use every 3 to 4 days for up to 8 weeks, with assessment if symptoms worsen or fail to improve in 2 to 4 weeks. The ciclopirox 1% label specifies 3 minutes, twice weekly for 4 weeks, at least 3 days apart. Do not apply one shampoo’s timer or prescription regimen to another product. A clinician can review persistent symptoms; patchy hair loss or an uncertain diagnosis may need an in-person scalp examination.

dental-pain-guide.question: What can a doctor prescribe for dental pain, and when are antibiotics needed?
dental-pain-guide.answerHtml: A telemedicine physician can manage dental pain as bridge care until dentist access is available but cannot perform dental procedures. The 2024 ADA guideline makes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, alone or combined with acetaminophen, first-line therapy for acute dental pain, and found they likely give better pain relief with a more favorable safety profile than opioids. The ADA antibiotic guideline (2019) recommends against antibiotics in most toothache scenarios and recommends them when the infection causes systemic involvement such as fever or malaise; it also suggests them for a localized abscess when dental treatment is not immediately available. When antibiotics are indicated, it suggests amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day or penicillin VK 500 mg four times a day for 3 to 7 days. For penicillin allergy the guideline lists cephalexin, azithromycin, or clindamycin, and notes that clindamycin carries a greater risk of C. difficile infection. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

dog-bite-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a dog bite wound and prevent infection?
dog-bite-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Infected dog bites usually grow several kinds of bacteria, and Pasteurella species are the most frequent isolates, according to a multicenter emergency department study. Per the CDC, care starts with immediate and thorough cleansing of the wound with soap and water. The 2014 IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline recommends 3 to 5 days of early antibiotics for higher-risk patients and wounds, such as people who are immunocompromised or have no spleen and moderate to severe injuries, especially to the hand or face, with amoxicillin-clavulanate as the usual choice. Under the CDC rabies algorithm, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is not indicated if the dog is healthy and stays healthy through a 10-day observation. Because bites are dirty wounds, the CDC recommends a tetanus vaccine if your last dose was 5 or more years ago. Go to the ER for deep facial lacerations or suspected tendon involvement. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in person.

doxy-pep-guide.question: What is doxy PEP and does it prevent STIs?
doxy-pep-guide.answerHtml: Doxy PEP (doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis) is a single 200 mg dose of the antibiotic doxycycline taken as soon as possible, and within 72 hours, after oral, vaginal, or anal sex to reduce the risk of syphilis, chlamydia, and gonorrhea, with no more than 200 mg in any 24 hours. The 2024 CDC clinical guidelines recommend that providers counsel gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men and transgender women who have had at least one bacterial STI in the past 12 months about doxy PEP and offer it through shared decision-making. Across three large randomized trials, including the 2023 DoxyPEP trial in the New England Journal of Medicine, 200 mg of doxycycline taken within 72 hours reduced syphilis and chlamydia by more than 70 percent and gonorrhea by about 50 percent. It does not prevent HIV. CDC makes no recommendation for cisgender women or cisgender heterosexual men because the evidence is insufficient to weigh benefits and harms in those groups. A licensed clinician can assess whether doxy PEP is appropriate and set up the recommended STI and HIV testing every 3 to 6 months.

ear-infection-guide.question: How do you treat swimmer's ear in an adult?
ear-infection-guide.answerHtml: For a stable adult with confirmed, uncomplicated swimmer’s ear, the AAO-HNSF guideline recommends a suitable topical ear preparation and pain relief rather than routine oral antibiotics. The cited US labels give seven-day external-ear courses: ofloxacin 0.3%, ten drops once daily for ages 13 and older, or ciprofloxacin/dexamethasone, four drops twice daily. An ear exam matters: if the eardrum may be perforated, use a non-ototoxic choice and avoid home drying drops. If treatment is not working within 48 to 72 hours, the guideline advises reassessment. Pain that is severe, spreading, or accompanied by high-risk symptoms needs in-person care.

eczema-atopic-dermatitis-guide.question: How is eczema (atopic dermatitis) treated in 2026?
eczema-atopic-dermatitis-guide.answerHtml: Eczema is common: around 31.6 million people in the U.S. have some form of eczema, according to the National Eczema Association. Atopic dermatitis, its most common form, is a chronic inflammatory skin disease linked to skin barrier dysfunction. The 2025 AAD focused update added strong recommendations for tapinarof cream, roflumilast cream, lebrikizumab, and nemolizumab (with topical therapy). Care usually steps up from moisturizers and trigger avoidance, to topical anti-inflammatories (corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, PDE-4 or JAK inhibitor creams), to phototherapy or systemic therapy, such as biologics (dupilumab and others) or oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, abrocitinib), for disease that topicals do not control. Oral JAK inhibitors are labeled for refractory disease and carry an FDA boxed warning. In two NEJM phase 3 trials, 36% to 38% of adults on dupilumab every other week reached clear or almost clear skin at 16 weeks, versus 8% to 10% on placebo. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

epinephrine-auto-injector-guide.question: How do you use an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and when is it needed?
epinephrine-auto-injector-guide.answerHtml: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, and antihistamines should never be used in place of it (Prince et al., 2018). Give it at the first sign of suspected anaphylaxis; the 2023 AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameter says meeting formal diagnostic criteria is not required first. The FDA labels for EpiPen and Auvi-Q set the dose by weight: 0.3 mg for 30 kg or more, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg, and Auvi-Q 0.1 mg for 7.5 to 15 kg, injected into the outer thigh, through clothing if needed. Keep two devices with you; a second dose can be used if symptoms continue or come back (Auvi-Q: starting 5 minutes after the first). The EpiPen label says to get emergency medical help right away after use, because symptoms can return hours later: 4.7% of reactions were biphasic in a large registry. A licensed clinician, reached by telehealth or in person, provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

erectile-dysfunction-guide.question: What is the best treatment for erectile dysfunction in 2026?
erectile-dysfunction-guide.answerHtml: Between 30 million and 50 million U.S. men have erectile dysfunction, according to NIDDK, and it often shares causes with heart disease. A 2021 BJU International umbrella review found ED predicts cardiovascular disease (RR 1.45), coronary heart disease (RR 1.50), and stroke (RR 1.36), and the 2024 Princeton IV Consensus tells clinicians to treat men with ED as at risk for cardiac events until proven otherwise. The AUA guideline (2018) presents every treatment that is not contraindicated as a potential first-line option, chosen through shared decision-making. PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, avanafil) are the most common first treatment, and generic sildenafil and tadalafil are widely available. A 2023 Journal of Sexual Medicine meta-analysis found aerobic exercise improves IIEF-EF scores by about 2.8 points. In the 2023 NEJM TRAVERSE trial, testosterone therapy in hypogonadal men at high cardiovascular risk was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiac events. The FDA warns that many sexual enhancement products are likely to be contaminated with dangerous hidden ingredients. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review symptoms, screen cardiovascular risk, and recommend appropriate therapy.

fda-compounded-glp1-503b-proposal.question: What does the FDA's 2026 proposal to remove GLP-1 drugs from the 503B compounding list mean for patients?
fda-compounded-glp1-503b-proposal.answerHtml: On April 30, 2026, the FDA proposed excluding semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list, finding no clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound these drugs from bulk substances. The Federal Register notice was published May 1, 2026, and the FDA later extended the comment period to July 30, 2026. As of November 15, 2026, we found no final determination, so it remains a proposal. The proposal does not immediately stop all compounding: patient-specific 503A compounding is still allowed under narrow conditions, and the FDA has said the tirzepatide and semaglutide injection shortages were resolved in December 2024 and February 2025. As of May 31, 2026, the FDA had received 990 adverse event reports associated with compounded semaglutide and more than 730 associated with compounded tirzepatide, including dosing errors, some requiring hospitalization. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

genital-herpes-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat genital herpes (HSV-2)?
genital-herpes-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Genital herpes (HSV-2) affects an estimated 11.9% of people aged 14 to 49 in the United States. The 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines list valacyclovir 1 g twice daily, acyclovir 400 mg three times daily, or famciclovir 250 mg three times daily, each for 7 to 10 days, for a first episode. Daily suppressive therapy reduces recurrences by 70% to 80% in people with frequent outbreaks, and in a randomized trial of 1,484 discordant couples, daily valacyclovir 500 mg roughly halved HSV-2 acquisition (hazard ratio 0.52). Episodic therapy (for example, valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily for 3 days) works best when started within 1 day of symptoms. Most genital herpes is transmitted by people who are unaware of their infection or have no symptoms at the time; condoms and antivirals reduce but do not eliminate risk. In pregnancy, CDC recommends suppressive therapy starting at 36 weeks for women with recurrent genital herpes, and cesarean delivery when recurrent lesions are present at the onset of labor. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

genital-warts-guide.question: What is the best treatment for genital warts (HPV) in 2026?
genital-warts-guide.answerHtml: Anogenital warts are a common sexually transmitted condition, and about 90% are caused by HPV types 6 or 11, which are nononcogenic (not cancer-causing) types (CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines). CDC lists several recommended treatments and states that no definitive evidence shows any one is superior, so the choice depends on wart size, number and location, patient preference, cost, convenience, side effects and clinician experience. Patient-applied options are imiquimod cream (5% at bedtime three times a week for up to 16 weeks, or 3.75% nightly for up to 8 weeks), podofilox 0.5% solution or gel (twice daily for 3 days, then 4 days off, up to four cycles), and sinecatechins 15% ointment (Veregen) (three times daily for up to 16 weeks). In trials, imiquimod 2% or 5% cream cleared warts in 51% of HIV-negative patients versus 6% with placebo (Moore 2001), and sinecatechins 15% in 57.2% versus 33.7% with vehicle (Tatti 2008). Provider-applied options are cryotherapy, trichloroacetic or bichloroacetic acid (TCA or BCA) 80% to 90%, and surgical removal; in one randomized trial in 130 men, warts resolved in 88% with cryotherapy and 81% with TCA (Godley 1987). Warts often recur after any treatment, especially in the first 3 months. The Gardasil 9 vaccine is FDA-approved for ages 9 through 45 and prevents genital warts caused by HPV 6 and 11 (FDA label). Podofilox and sinecatechins should not be used during pregnancy, and CDC advises avoiding imiquimod in pregnancy until more data are available. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can prescribe the patient-applied treatments and coordinate provider-applied treatment when needed.

gig-worker-healthcare-options.question: What are the healthcare options for gig workers without employer insurance?
gig-worker-healthcare-options.answerHtml: In a July 2023 federal survey, 11.9 million people worked as independent contractors, and they were less likely than workers in traditional jobs to have health insurance from any source (74.2% vs 84.9%), according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Realistic options include ACA Marketplace plans at HealthCare.gov, where savings are based on your income estimate, and Medicaid, which in expansion states covers adults with income at or below 138% of the federal poverty level, according to CMS. Health sharing ministries are not insurance, and short-term plans can deny coverage for pre-existing conditions. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

glp-1-weight-loss-oral-medication-guide.question: What are the GLP-1 weight loss medications available in 2026, including oral options?
glp-1-weight-loss-oral-medication-guide.answerHtml: In their pivotal trials, injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg lowered body weight by an average of 14.9% (STEP 1, NEJM) and tirzepatide 15 mg by 20.9% (SURMOUNT-1, NEJM). The FDA approved Foundayo (orforglipron) on April 1, 2026, as a once-daily GLP-1 pill that does not need to be taken on an empty stomach (FDA); in the ATTAIN-1 trial, orforglipron 36 mg lowered weight by 11.2% at 72 weeks versus 2.1% with placebo (NEJM, 2025). Foundayo carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or with MEN 2. One year after stopping semaglutide, trial participants had regained two-thirds of the weight they had lost (STEP 1 extension). As of November 7, 2026, Lilly lists self-pay Foundayo starting at $149 per month for the lowest dose (LillyDirect). A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

gout-guide.question: What is the best treatment for gout in 2026?
gout-guide.answerHtml: Acute gout flares are treated promptly with an anti-inflammatory selected for the person's medical history: low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg one hour later), an NSAID at an anti-inflammatory dose, or a short oral corticosteroid course. Long-term control requires urate-lowering therapy when indicated, usually allopurinol started low and titrated to serum urate below 6 mg/dL. The 2020 ACR guideline strongly recommends urate-lowering therapy for tophi, gout-related radiographic damage, or two or more flares yearly. Before allopurinol, people of Southeast Asian or African American ancestry should discuss HLA-B*58:01 testing because the allele is associated with severe skin reactions. A first hot, swollen joint or fever needs urgent in-person assessment to exclude infection.

hair-loss-male-pattern-guide.question: What is the best treatment for male pattern hair loss in 2026?
hair-loss-male-pattern-guide.answerHtml: For most men with androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss), the best-supported medicines are oral finasteride 1 mg daily, which is FDA-approved for male pattern hair loss, and topical minoxidil 5% twice daily (finasteride prescribing information; minoxidil 5% Drug Facts label). European evidence-based guidelines recommend both, as summarized in a phase III trial report (Piraccini 2022). In a meta-analysis of five randomized trials, using them together gave better global photographic scores than either drug alone, with similar side effects, although the change in hair density did not differ significantly (Chen 2020). Low-dose oral minoxidil (usual starting dose 1 to 5 mg daily in men) lacks FDA approval for hair loss but has been reported as an effective, well-tolerated alternative for healthy patients having difficulty with topical minoxidil (Skin Appendage Disord 2023 review; Randolph 2021). Finasteride usually needs three months or more of daily use before benefit is seen, and stopping it reverses the effect within 12 months. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can start finasteride and minoxidil after reviewing medical history.

head-lice-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat head lice in an adult, and when should you retreat?
head-lice-treatment-guide.answerHtml: For adults, start head-lice treatment by confirming an active infestation, ideally with a live crawling louse, rather than itching or old nits alone. Three commonly discussed products have 10-minute application instructions but different retreatment rules: the cited permethrin 1% label calls for another application if live lice are seen seven days or more later; the ivermectin 0.5% label says not to repeat for the same infestation without talking to a healthcare provider; and the spinosad 0.9% label repeats only if live lice remain at day seven. Ten minutes is contact time, not proof of cure. CDC guidance advises clinician review if lice remain as active as before treatment, rather than immediate extra dosing. Recheck the diagnosis, technique and exposure before assuming resistance.

hyperhidrosis-guide.question: What is the best treatment for hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) in 2026?
hyperhidrosis-guide.answerHtml: Hyperhidrosis affects an estimated 4.8% of the U.S. population (about 15.3 million people), yet only 51% of those affected had discussed it with a healthcare professional (Doolittle et al., Arch Dermatol Res 2016). The Canadian Hyperhidrosis Advisory Committee severity-based algorithm starts mild (HDSS score 2) axillary, palmar, or plantar disease on topical aluminum chloride, with botulinum toxin A (axillae, palms, soles) and iontophoresis (palms, soles) as second-line therapy if that fails; in severe disease (HDSS score 3 or 4), botulinum toxin A and topical aluminum chloride are both first-line. Topical glycopyrronium (Qbrexza) and sofpironium gel (Sofdra) are FDA-approved for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in patients 9 years of age and older (Qbrexza label; Sofdra label). Oral anticholinergics such as oxybutynin are off-label options reserved for treatment-resistant or generalized sweating (Nawrocki and Cha, J Am Acad Dermatol 2019). miraDry (microwave thermolysis) is FDA-cleared for the underarms, and endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy is the treatment of last resort because of compensatory sweating. Every serious attempt at treating excessive sweating starts with confirming primary versus secondary hyperhidrosis. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth, can start most first-line and second-line therapies without an in-person visit.

hypertension-blood-pressure-guide.question: How is hypertension treated, and when can I get a blood pressure medication refill via telehealth?
hypertension-blood-pressure-guide.answerHtml: Nearly half of US adults (47.7%) have hypertension, but only about 1 in 5 of them (20.7%) have it controlled below 130/80 mmHg (CDC NCHS Data Brief 511). Under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline the goal is below 130/80 mmHg for most adults, and first-line medicines are thiazide-type diuretics, long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors and ARBs (Hypertension, 2025). In the DASH-Sodium trial, the DASH diet plus lower sodium lowered systolic BP by about 5 to 21 mmHg depending on the starting level (JACC, 2017). A BP higher than 180/120 with symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath or vision change is a hypertensive emergency: call 911 (American Heart Association). Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in-person.

hypothyroidism-treatment-guide.question: How is hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, and how should TSH be monitored?
hypothyroidism-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Clinical hypothyroidism affects about 1 in 300 people in the US, and Hashimoto’s disease is the most common cause (Wilson, Am Fam Physician 2021). Levothyroxine remains the standard of care (ATA 2014 guidelines). The Synthroid label gives a full replacement dose of 1.6 mcg/kg/day, with a lower starting dose for older adults and people with heart disease; it advises checking TSH 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change and every 6 to 12 months once the dose is stable (Synthroid label, DailyMed). Take it on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before eating, and 4 hours apart from drugs that reduce absorption, such as calcium and iron. Women who become pregnant usually need about 30% more, often taken as 9 doses per week, with TSH checked every 4 weeks (Wilson, Am Fam Physician 2021). Stable, uncomplicated cases are often suited to telehealth follow-up; red-flag symptoms need in-person or emergency care.

international-visitor-medical-care-guide.question: What should international visitors do if they get sick in the United States?
international-visitor-medical-care-guide.answerHtml: In 2024 there were 72.4 million international visitor arrivals to the United States (U.S. National Travel and Tourism Office), and some visitors get sick during the trip. The US has no universal healthcare system, so visitors navigate four main access points: 911 for life-threatening emergencies, the emergency department for genuine emergencies, urgent care for same-day non-emergencies, and telehealth for conditions that do not require an in-person exam. Prices are not standardized; uninsured or self-pay patients must be given a good faith estimate when they schedule care or ask for one, and can dispute a bill that is at least $400 above it (CMS). Under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, covered entities such as hospitals must provide language assistance free of charge and offer a qualified interpreter when one is requested (HHS Office for Civil Rights). Federal law requires a prescription from a practitioner licensed by law to administer the drug, so plan on a US-licensed clinician writing a new one (21 U.S.C. 353(b)(1)), and foreign visitors may bring up to 50 dosage units of controlled substances for personal use in their original labeled containers (DEA guidance). Travelers’ diarrhea (attack rates 30 to 70 percent of travelers over two weeks, depending on destination and season; CDC Yellow Book), respiratory infections, UTIs, minor injuries, and prescription refills can often be handled outside the ER.

latisse-guide.question: How does Latisse (bimatoprost) work for eyelash growth, and does it actually work?
latisse-guide.answerHtml: Latisse (bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03%) is a prescription drug approved by the FDA in December 2008 to treat hypotrichosis of the eyelashes (inadequate or not enough lashes) by increasing their growth, including length, thickness and darkness. Bimatoprost was first developed as a glaucoma eye drop. Applied once nightly to the skin of the upper eyelid margin with a sterile applicator, it is believed to work by increasing the percentage of lashes in the anagen (growth) phase and the length of that phase. In the pivotal trial of 278 adults, 78% of bimatoprost-treated patients had at least a one-grade improvement on the Global Eyelash Assessment at 16 weeks, versus 18% with vehicle (Smith et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2012). According to the FDA-approved label, mean eyelash length rose 25% from baseline versus 2% with vehicle, the effect is not significant in most patients until 2 months, and eyelash growth is expected to return to its pre-treatment level after stopping. The most common side effects (about 3% to 4% of patients) are eye itching, eye redness and skin darkening, and the label warns that increased brown iris pigmentation can occur and is likely to be permanent. A licensed clinician can prescribe Latisse after reviewing eye health and medical history, including any glaucoma eye drops.

malaria-prophylaxis-guide.question: What is the difference between Malarone and doxycycline for malaria prevention?
malaria-prophylaxis-guide.answerHtml: Both atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) and doxycycline are first-line options for chloroquine-resistant malaria per the CDC malaria drug-selection guidelines. The primary difference is post-trip duration: Malarone continues for only 7 days after leaving the malaria zone (ideal for shorter trips), while doxycycline requires 4 full weeks after return (the most common adherence failure). Doxycycline is substantially less expensive and is preferred for Thai border regions. Key contraindications differ: doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy (all trimesters) and children under 8; Malarone is avoided in severe renal impairment. Doxycycline requires daily SPF 30+ sunscreen due to photosensitivity. Per the DailyMed doxycycline label, both begin 1–2 days before entering the malaria zone.

managing-blood-pressure-mobile-workers.question: How can truck drivers and mobile workers manage high blood pressure while on the road?
managing-blood-pressure-mobile-workers.answerHtml: Under FMCSA medical examiner guidance, a driver with blood pressure below 140/90 may be certified for up to 2 years (at least yearly if treated for hypertension); 140/90 to 159/99 allows 1 year; 160/100 to 179/109 allows a one-time 3-month certificate; and 180/110 or higher means no certification until blood pressure is 140/90 or less (FMCSA). The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline goal for most adults is below 130/80, and its first-line medicines are thiazide-type diuretics, long-acting calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors and ARBs (Hypertension, 2025). Common options such as amlodipine, lisinopril, losartan and chlorthalidone are labeled for once-daily dosing. Blood pressure higher than 180/120 with symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, numbness, weakness, vision change or difficulty speaking means call 911 (American Heart Association). A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

mastitis-treatment-guide.question: How is mastitis treated, and should you continue breastfeeding?
mastitis-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Mastitis is a spectrum that runs from ductal narrowing and inflammatory mastitis to bacterial mastitis, phlegmon and abscess, and the ABM Protocol #36 (2022) advises reserving antibiotics for bacterial mastitis. Keep breastfeeding: ABM states that bacterial mastitis does not pose a risk to the infant and does not require an interruption in breastfeeding. When antibiotics are needed, ABM lists first-line dicloxacillin (or flucloxacillin) 500 mg four times daily or cephalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 to 14 days; Cleveland Clinic clinicians advise antibiotics when systemic symptoms such as fever, body aches or shaking chills (rigors) do not improve within 24 to 48 hours of conservative care. About 3 to 11% of people with acute mastitis develop a breast abscess, which needs drainage. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or an in-person visit, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

medical-care-visitors-from-india-guide.question: How can a visitor from India keep their prescriptions and chronic conditions on track during a US trip?
medical-care-visitors-from-india-guide.answerHtml: For the 2.2 million visitors who traveled from India to the US in 2024 (NTTO 2024), two common medical questions are how to keep a chronic-condition regimen intact and whether a foreign prescription can be filled here. In short: carry a list of your medicines by generic name, as the CDC Yellow Book advises; US federal law allows a prescription drug to be dispensed only on the prescription of a practitioner licensed by law (21 U.S.C. 353(b)), so plan on a US-licensed clinician writing any new US prescription; and under the FDA personal importation policy foreign nationals may bring or ship a 90-day supply of drug products. Alprazolam (Restyl), modafinil (Modalert), clonazepam, diazepam and nitrazepam are Schedule IV controlled substances in the US (21 CFR 1308.14), and foreign visitors may bring up to 50 dosage units of controlled substances for personal use (DEA); flunitrazepam (Rohypnol) has never been approved for medical use in the US (DEA). For older visiting parents the clinical picture also matters: South Asians in the US had 23% age-adjusted diabetes prevalence compared with 6% in non-Hispanic Whites (Kanaya et al. 2014, MASALA/MESA), diabetes was diagnosed about 10 years earlier in a California survey (Becerra and Becerra 2015), and the 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline lists South Asian ancestry among its risk-enhancing factors.

medical-care-visitors-from-mexico-guide.question: How can a visitor from Mexico keep their prescriptions and chronic conditions on track during a US trip?
medical-care-visitors-from-mexico-guide.answerHtml: In 2024, 13.4 million Mexicans visited the US by land (NTTO 2024). Federal law requires prescription drugs to be dispensed on the prescription of a practitioner licensed by law (21 U.S.C. 353(b)), so a Mexican prescription generally cannot be filled at a US pharmacy; a visit with a US-licensed clinician, including by telehealth, can result in a US prescription for non-controlled chronic medications (blood pressure, thyroid, oral diabetes, statins, most inhalers) if the clinician judges it appropriate. Under the FDA Personal Importation Policy foreign nationals may bring or ship a 90-day supply of drug products, and FDA says a drug approved in another country but unapproved in the US is illegal to import. Some medications commonly prescribed in Mexico are US Schedule IV controlled substances (Rivotril / clonazepam, Tafil / alprazolam, Ambien / zolpidem, tramadol), and DEA allows foreign visitors to bring up to 50 dosage units of controlled substances for personal use (DEA). Per the CDC National Diabetes Statistics Report, crude diagnosed diabetes prevalence among Mexican or Mexican American adults was 11.1% (2019-2021), compared with 13.3% in Puerto Rican adults and 8.5% in non-Hispanic White adults. Entities covered by Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, such as hospitals that receive federal financial assistance, must provide language assistance free of charge, including qualified interpreters (HHS OCR letter, December 2024; full implementation by July 5, 2025).

migraine-treatment-guide.question: What are the best treatments for migraines, including prevention?
migraine-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Migraine is the leading cause of disability in people under 50, according to a review of Global Burden of Disease data (Steiner et al., J Headache Pain 2018). Acetaminophen and oral NSAIDs are first-line for mild to moderate attacks, triptans are an effective first-line treatment for moderate to severe attacks, and medication works best when taken early in the attack (Am Fam Physician 2018). Using triptans on 10 or more days a month (ICHD-3 8.2.2), or non-opioid pain relievers on 15 or more days a month (ICHD-3 8.2.3), for more than 3 months can cause medication overuse headache. Preventive therapy should be considered with four or more headaches a month (Am Fam Physician 2019), and the 2024 American Headache Society position statement says CGRP-targeting therapies should be considered first-line for prevention without prior failure of other drug classes (Charles et al., Headache 2024). A sudden thunderclap headache needs emergency evaluation because its most common secondary cause is subarachnoid hemorrhage (Chen and Fuh, Curr Opin Neurol 2021). A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and decide on appropriate therapy.

motion-sickness-treatment-guide.question: Which motion-sickness medicine should an adult choose before travel?
motion-sickness-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Choose prevention by the active ingredient, time before travel and safety risks. A scopolamine patch is applied at least 4 hours ahead and worn for up to 3 days. Meclizine and dimenhydrinate have different directions and can cause drowsiness. Avoid alcohol and doubling up medicines. Medicines generally work best before motion starts. Severe confusion, overheating, eye pain or new neurological symptoms need direct assessment, not another dose.[1][2][4][5][6][13]

paxlovid-2026-efficacy-update.question: Does Paxlovid still work in 2026, and who benefits most?
paxlovid-2026-efficacy-update.answerHtml: Real-world data from 703,647 patients show Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) reduced hospitalization by 39% and death by 61%, including among vaccinated patients in the Omicron era (Bhatia et al., PLoS Medicine, 2025). Absolute benefit depends on baseline risk: in that study the absolute reductions were 0.9 percentage points for hospitalization and 0.2 for death, with a much greater benefit in people 65 and older. In a trial of vaccinated adults with at least one risk factor and unvaccinated adults without risk factors, hospitalization or death occurred in 0.8% with Paxlovid vs 1.6% with placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant (Hammond et al., NEJM, 2024). Virologic rebound occurred in about 1 in 5 treated patients in one Boston cohort (Edelstein et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2023), and in a randomized trial a second course after rebound sped viral decline but showed no clear clinical benefit (Zhang et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases). The FDA label says to start treatment within 5 days of symptom onset (Paxlovid prescribing information). A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

performance-anxiety-treatment-guide.question: Can propranolol help performance anxiety?
performance-anxiety-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Propranolol is a beta-blocker that blunts the body's adrenaline response: racing heart, shaky hands, trembling voice and sweating. Taken as a single dose before a speech, audition, interview or exam, it can reduce those physical symptoms without sedation. In a double-blind study of musicians, beta blockade reduced the physical symptoms of stage fright, and music critics rated performance quality higher (Brantigan et al., American Journal of Medicine, 1982). It treats the body's symptoms, not the anxious thoughts. A 2019 systematic review of 43 studies in professional musicians found cognitive behavioral therapy and beta-blockers were the most studied treatments, with beneficial results for CBT, and noted the studies had methodological weaknesses (Fernholz et al., Psychological Medicine, 2019). For an ongoing anxiety disorder, a 2016 meta-analysis concluded the evidence was insufficient to support routine propranolol use (Steenen et al., 2016). Propranolol is not safe for everyone: the FDA label lists it as contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia and greater than first degree heart block, bronchial asthma, and known hypersensitivity to propranolol (propranolol tablets label, DailyMed, revised January 2026). Performance anxiety is not one of the label's indications, so this use is off-label, and a physician decides whether it fits you. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

pink-eye-adults-antibiotics-vs-watchful-.question: Do adults with pink eye need antibiotic eye drops, or is watchful waiting appropriate?
pink-eye-adults-antibiotics-vs-watchful-.answerHtml: Viruses cause up to 80% of acute conjunctivitis, antibiotics do not help viral pink eye, and at least 60% of bacterial cases are self-limited without treatment, per a JAMA systematic review. For bacterial conjunctivitis, a Cochrane review of 21 RCTs (8,805 participants) (2023) found antibiotics likely improve clinical cure modestly: 68.2% of antibiotic-treated participants versus 55.5% on placebo had resolved by days 4 to 9. In a randomized trial in UK general practice, a delayed prescription cut antibiotic use to 53% (versus 99% with immediate antibiotics) with similar symptom severity, and an American Family Physician review calls delaying antibiotics an option for many patients. Per the same review, antibiotic therapy should be considered for purulent or mucopurulent discharge, marked discomfort, contact lens wear, a weakened immune system, or suspected chlamydial or gonococcal infection (these two need systemic treatment); erythromycin ointment and polymyxin-trimethoprim drops are examples labeled for bacterial eye-surface infections. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

pink-eye-conjunctivitis-guide.question: What is pink eye (conjunctivitis) and how is it treated?
pink-eye-conjunctivitis-guide.answerHtml: Pink eye (conjunctivitis) affects an estimated 6 million people in the United States each year and is classified as viral (about 80% of infectious cases), bacterial, or allergic. The 2024 American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern says indiscriminate use of topical antibiotics should be avoided, because viral conjunctivitis will not respond to antibacterial agents and mild bacterial conjunctivitis is likely to be self-limited. Viral conjunctivitis is managed with cold compresses and artificial tears; antibiotic drops should be considered for purulent or mucopurulent bacterial conjunctivitis; antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer drops relieve allergic conjunctivitis symptoms. Red flags that need prompt in-person care include vision loss, moderate or severe pain, severe purulent discharge, and corneal involvement. A licensed clinician can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps, by telehealth or in person.

poison-ivy-oak-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a poison ivy, oak, or sumac rash?
poison-ivy-oak-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Urushiol, the oily sap in poison ivy, oak, and sumac, causes a rash in 80 to 90% of adults exposed to an amount smaller than a grain of salt, according to NIOSH. Wash exposed skin with soap and cool water as soon as possible after contact, per the FDA. Mild rashes can be eased with hydrocortisone cream or lotion, calamine lotion, and cool compresses, per AAD guidance. Oral or intramuscular steroids may be prescribed for severe blistering, a rash on the face, hands, or genitals, or involvement of more than 20% of the skin, per the JAMA Patient Page; for severe poison ivy, American Family Physician guidance advises tapering oral prednisone over two to three weeks because rapid discontinuation can cause rebound dermatitis. Inhaling smoke from burning plants can cause severe allergic respiratory problems. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

psoriasis-treatment-guide.question: How is psoriasis treated according to current clinical guidelines?
psoriasis-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Psoriasis treatment follows the AAD-NPF joint guidelines, which recommend topical corticosteroids for plaque psoriasis outside skin folds, note that off-label topical calcineurin inhibitors work on the face and genitals, and cover phototherapy, oral systemic drugs, and biologics for more extensive disease. FDA labels approve IL-17 and IL-23 biologics such as risankizumab for adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis who are candidates for systemic therapy or phototherapy; in its label trials, 75% of patients reached PASI 90 at week 16. The guidelines recommend PASI for clinical trials rather than routine practice. Rheumatologists diagnosed psoriatic arthritis in 30% of dermatology patients with plaque psoriasis in a large study, so joint screening matters. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

rosacea-treatment-guide.question: How is rosacea treated, and where does azelaic acid 15% fit?
rosacea-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Rosacea treatment is matched to the features present. For inflammatory bumps, options include azelaic acid, ivermectin, and metronidazole, as outlined by the American Academy of Dermatology. Prescription azelaic acid 15% gel or foam is used for mild-to-moderate inflammatory papules and pustules; the gel label does not establish efficacy for redness alone. Both cited US formulations are used twice daily under their labels, with reassessment if there is no improvement after 12 weeks. OTC 10% products are not established as interchangeable with these prescription formulations. A licensed clinician can assess uncomplicated skin symptoms by an appropriate video or in-person visit; eye symptoms, uncertain diagnoses, and complex disease need appropriate in-person care.

running-out-of-medication-visiting-us-gu.question: What should an international visitor do if they run out of medication in the United States?
running-out-of-medication-visiting-us-gu.answerHtml: International visitors who run out of a chronic medication during a US trip should not count on a US pharmacy filling a prescription written abroad. Federal rules allow a controlled-substance prescription to come only from a practitioner registered with, or exempted by, the DEA (21 CFR 1306.03), and for other medicines it depends on state law, so the usual fix is a new prescription from a US-licensed clinician. A physician-led telehealth visit is one common way to get one for non-controlled medications like blood pressure pills, thyroid hormone, oral diabetes drugs, most asthma inhalers, statins, birth control pills, and most SSRIs. Under the FDA Personal Importation Policy, foreign nationals may bring or ship a 90-day supply of their medication, and those staying longer than 90 days may have additional medication sent to them. DEA's traveler handout says foreign visitors may bring up to 50 dosage units of controlled substances (such as opioids, benzodiazepines, ADHD stimulants, and sleep medications) for personal use in the original container, and that all medications should be declared at US customs (DEA 2026). DEA telemedicine flexibilities extended through December 31, 2026 allow DEA-registered US clinicians to prescribe Schedule II-V controlled medications via audio-video telemedicine without a prior in-person visit, provided the prescriptions comply with applicable federal and state law, but individual telehealth companies often apply stricter internal rules and frequently decline controlled prescriptions for visitors. Generic prices differ between US pharmacies, so compare prices with a service such as GoodRx before you fill.

scabies-treatment-guide.question: How is scabies diagnosed and treated?
scabies-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Scabies is a highly contagious skin infestation caused by the human itch mite, Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Per CDC clinical guidance, permethrin 5% cream is applied from the neck down and washed off after 8 to 14 hours, and a second application about a week later may be needed. Oral ivermectin, which is not FDA approved for scabies, is given as two doses of 200 mcg/kg with food, 7 to 14 days apart; its safety has not been established in pregnancy or in children weighing less than 15 kg. CDC advises treating all household members and close contacts at the same time as the person with scabies. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is treated with oral ivermectin together with a topical agent, often as 3, 5, or 7 doses depending on severity, and warrants in-person evaluation. Itching can continue for several weeks after treatment even when all the mites and eggs are killed. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

seasonal-allergies-guide.question: How are seasonal allergies (allergic rhinitis) treated?
seasonal-allergies-guide.answerHtml: About one in four U.S. adults (25.2%) had a diagnosed seasonal allergy in 2024, according to CDC's National Center for Health Statistics. The Rhinitis 2020 practice parameter update calls intranasal corticosteroid sprays the preferred single medicine for persistent allergic rhinitis. The AAO-HNSF clinical practice guideline strongly recommends intranasal steroids when symptoms affect quality of life, strongly recommends second-generation oral antihistamines (such as cetirizine, loratadine, or fexofenadine) when sneezing and itching are the main complaints, and recommends offering allergen immunotherapy when medicines do not adequately control symptoms. The ARIA-EAACI 2024-2025 guideline revision suggests a fixed combination of an intranasal antihistamine and corticosteroid (for example, azelastine-fluticasone) over either medicine alone, as a conditional recommendation. A licensed clinician, reached via telehealth or an in-person visit, provides the clinical judgment AI tools cannot.

seasonal-allergy-guidelines-2026.question: What changed in the 2026 seasonal allergy treatment guidelines?
seasonal-allergy-guidelines-2026.answerHtml: The main guideline update is the ARIA-EAACI 2024-2025 revision, published in the journal Allergy in two parts: Part I on intranasal treatments (PubMed date December 2025) and Part II on oral and eye treatments (March 2026). Part I suggests a combination intranasal antihistamine and corticosteroid spray (INAH+INCS), such as azelastine-fluticasone, over either spray alone, as a conditional recommendation. Part II recommends an intranasal corticosteroid over an oral antihistamine, an oral antihistamine over montelukast, and second-generation over first-generation oral antihistamines. A 2024 meta-analysis of 151 studies in JACI found azelastine-fluticasone, fluticasone furoate and fluticasone propionate most likely to give moderate or large improvements in seasonal allergic rhinitis. North American pollen seasons lengthened by about 20 days from 1990 to 2018. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

shingles-antiviral-window-guide.question: Which antivirals treat shingles, and how soon should you start?
shingles-antiviral-window-guide.answerHtml: CDC names three preferred antiviral drugs for shingles: acyclovir, valacyclovir and famciclovir. Treatment is most effective within 72 hours of symptom onset, and the FDA-labeled valacyclovir regimen is 1 gram three times daily for 7 days, started at the earliest sign of shingles. Do not wait for the clock if new blisters are forming or the rash affects the eye, face, ear, immune system, or nervous system. The valacyclovir trial and a clinical review of shingles care explain why timing and location both matter.

shingles-guide.question: How is shingles treated, and what is the 72-hour antiviral window?
shingles-guide.answerHtml: Shingles is a painful, one-sided rash caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. Oral antiviral treatment is best studied when started within 72 hours after rash onset.
