Valacyclovir, acyclovir, and famciclovir are options; eye, face, ear, widespread, neurologic, and immunocompromised cases need in-person evaluation. CDC's clinical overview and ACIP recommendations support prompt treatment and prevention with Shingrix when eligible.

shingles-vaccine-guide.question: Who should get Shingrix, and how effective is the shingles vaccine?
shingles-vaccine-guide.answerHtml: CDC recommends Shingrix, a two-dose, non-live vaccine, for immunocompetent adults age 50 and older and for adults age 19 and older who are or will be immunocompromised. Pivotal trials found 97.2% efficacy against shingles in adults age 50 and older and 91.3% in pooled adults age 70 and older. CDC's vaccine recommendations, the ZOE-50 trial and the ZOE-70 trial provide the core evidence.

sinus-infection-guide.question: When does an adult sinus infection need antibiotics?
sinus-infection-guide.answerHtml: Most sinus infections get better on their own without antibiotics.[8] Bacterial disease is more likely when symptoms last at least 10 days without improvement, worsen after initial improvement, or start severe.[2][7] Uncomplicated cases may use watchful waiting when reliable follow-up is available.[1][7] When an antibiotic is chosen, amoxicillin with or without clavulanate is first-line, and IDSA recommends 5 to 7 days for uncomplicated cases in adults.[1][2] Eye pain or swelling, vision changes, confusion or a stiff neck need care immediately.[17]

smoking-cessation-guide.question: What is the best treatment for smoking cessation in 2026?
smoking-cessation-guide.answerHtml: For most adults who smoke, a 2022 JAMA review recommends combining medication with behavioral support, with varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus lozenge or gum) as the preferred first choices. In the head-to-head EAGLES trial (8,144 participants), 6-month quit rates were 21.8% with varenicline, 16.2% with bupropion, 15.7% with the nicotine patch, and 9.4% with placebo, as reported in that review. A 2023 Cochrane review found high-certainty evidence that combination NRT works better than a single form (RR 1.27). The FDA removed varenicline’s boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events in December 2016; its current label still says to stop it and contact a clinician right away if mood or behavior changes. In the USPSTF 2021 evidence review, combined medication and behavioral support raised quit rates compared with minimal support or placebo (pooled RR 1.83). Cytisinicline remains investigational in the U.S.: the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter in June 2026 citing manufacturing and labeling issues, and the company reports no efficacy or safety deficiencies were identified. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review your history, screen for contraindications, and prescribe appropriate therapy.

sore-throat-guide.question: When does an adult sore throat need a strep test?
sore-throat-guide.answerHtml: For an adult sore throat, make 3 decisions: whether urgent assessment is needed, whether strep testing is appropriate, and whether a confirmed infection needs treatment. Group A strep causes about 5% to 15% of adult pharyngitis. White spots or a clinical score cannot confirm it. Clear viral symptoms usually do not need a strep test; other cases may need a throat swab before antibiotics.[1][2][5][6]

telehealth-acne-eczema-dermatology-evide.question: Is telehealth effective for treating acne and eczema?
telehealth-acne-eczema-dermatology-evide.answerHtml: Published studies suggest teledermatology can produce outcomes similar to in-person care for acne and eczema, especially for follow-up visits. In a randomized trial of 151 patients with mild to moderate acne, online follow-up visits gave lesion-count improvements similar to office visits (Archives of Dermatology, 2010). In a randomized trial of 156 children and adults with atopic dermatitis, online follow-up care after a first in-person visit gave equivalent improvements in eczema severity (JAMA Dermatology, 2015). A 2024 scoping review of 21 acne studies in the Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery found similar outcomes on several acne-grading scales but lower follow-up compliance with virtual care. Conditions requiring biopsy or patch testing need in-person referral. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

telehealth-ear-infections-adults.question: Can you treat an ear infection over telehealth?
telehealth-ear-infections-adults.answerHtml: Many uncomplicated adult ear infections can be assessed by video, but some need an in-person ear exam. In a 2022 UK pilot of 58 adults referred for hearing loss or tinnitus (not ear infections), remote review of smartphone otoscope images let 65% avoid any hospital attendance, with 95% diagnostic concordance and 98% satisfaction; 24% still needed a face-to-face appointment. The AAO-HNS guideline recommends topical ear drops, not oral antibiotics, as initial therapy for uncomplicated otitis externa (swimmer's ear). Fluid coming out of the ear, a change in hearing or new hearing loss, swelling around the ear, diabetes or a weakened immune system call for an urgent medical appointment. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

telehealth-sinusitis-virtual-care.question: Can a sinus infection be treated via telehealth?
telehealth-sinusitis-virtual-care.answerHtml: Often, yes. In a 2019 primary care network study in Open Forum Infectious Diseases, adults with sinusitis seen by virtual visit more often received a guideline-concordant diagnosis than those seen in the office (69.1% vs. 45.7%, P<.001) and were less often prescribed antibiotics (68.6% vs. 94.3%), although they returned for sinusitis more often within 24 hours and 30 days. The 2025 AAO-HNSF adult sinusitis guideline update extends watchful waiting (without antibiotics) to all adults with uncomplicated acute bacterial sinusitis; when an antibiotic is used, amoxicillin with or without clavulanate is first-line, for 5 to 7 days for most adults. Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement or severe facial pain call for a clinician's evaluation, and swelling around the eye, vision changes, a severe headache, a stiff neck, or confusion need urgent in-person or emergency care. A licensed clinician, by telehealth or in person, can review the symptoms and decide on appropriate therapy.

telehealth-uti-clinical-evidence.question: What does the clinical evidence show about telehealth for UTI treatment?
telehealth-uti-clinical-evidence.answerHtml: Published evidence on telehealth care for uncomplicated UTI in women is encouraging but mostly observational. A 2023 PLOS ONE analysis of 51,474 visits by adult women to one national telemedicine UTI program found that 89.7% of treated patients who answered a seven-day follow-up survey (3,521 people, about 7% of visits) reported symptom resolution, which the authors, who worked for the company that ran the program, described as similar to published in-person rates; 94% of treated patients received an antibiotic recommended by the program's clinical protocol, which was based on IDSA guidance. A 2026 PLOS Digital Health scoping review of 22 studies of drug prescribing found mixed results and no consensus on how virtual and in-person prescribing differ. Telehealth is appropriate for uncomplicated UTIs in non-pregnant women aged 18–65 without comorbidities; first-line options in the IDSA cystitis guideline include nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg (one double-strength tablet) twice daily for 3 days where local resistance does not exceed 20%. Red flags such as fever above 101°F, flank pain, or pregnancy require in-person care; fever, back or side pain, chills and vomiting can be signs of a kidney infection (MedlinePlus). A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

tick-bite-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat a tick bite and prevent Lyme disease?
tick-bite-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Remove the tick promptly with fine-tipped tweezers; the 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR guideline notes that most Borrelia burgdorferi transmission occurs after 36 to 48 hours of attachment. Per the 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR Lyme disease guidelines, a single oral dose of doxycycline (200 mg for adults) is recommended within 72 hours of tick removal only for a high-risk bite: an identified Ixodes tick, a highly endemic area, and attachment of 36 hours or more. In the 2001 trial behind the recommendation, efficacy was 87% (95% CI 25% to 98%). In 2022, 62,551 Lyme disease cases (confirmed and probable) were reported to CDC. An expanding erythema migrans rash is treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (IDSA recommends a 10-day course; CDC lists 10 to 14 days) without waiting for serology. Suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever needs doxycycline right away; delay in diagnosis and treatment is the most important factor associated with increased likelihood of death. Seek the ER for petechial rash, high fever, or meningismus. Telehealth is appropriate for prophylaxis assessment and early Lyme management. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

tinea-ringworm-guide.question: How do you treat ringworm and other tinea fungal skin infections?
tinea-ringworm-guide.answerHtml: Tinea (ringworm) is caused by dermatophyte fungi, and treatment depends on location. For tinea corporis and cruris, topical terbinafine 1% once daily for 1 to 2 weeks is a first-line option; over-the-counter clotrimazole 1% twice daily for 2 to 4 weeks is an alternative, although a 2025 review favors terbinafine or butenafine as more effective. Tinea capitis requires oral therapy because topical antifungals do not penetrate the hair follicle. In the US, where Trichophyton causes more than 89% of tinea capitis, oral terbinafine for 4 to 6 weeks is a reasonable first choice; griseofulvin may be needed when culture shows Microsporum. Onychomycosis: confirm with nail testing, then oral terbinafine 250 mg once daily for 6 weeks (fingernails) or 12 weeks (toenails). Avoid combination steroid-antifungal creams, which can mask the infection and let it spread (tinea incognito). Telehealth is appropriate for body and groin tinea; scalp infections and nail fungus can also be initiated virtually. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

tinea-versicolor-guide.question: How do you treat tinea versicolor and why does skin discoloration persist after treatment?
tinea-versicolor-guide.answerHtml: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia yeast, not a dermatophyte, so oral terbinafine is not effective. Topical medicine is the most common treatment, per the American Academy of Dermatology: for example, selenium sulfide 2.5% lotion left on for 10 minutes once a day for 7 days, or ketoconazole 2% shampoo left on for 5 minutes, with one application usually sufficient, per their US labels (selenium sulfide, ketoconazole shampoo). For extensive disease, a systematic review supports oral fluconazole 300 mg weekly for 2 weeks or itraconazole 200 mg daily for 5 or 7 days. Skin color can stay lighter or darker for weeks or months after the yeast is gone; lighter patches form because azelaic acid made by Malassezia inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase. Recurrence can reach as much as 60% in 1 year and 80% in 2 years, and the AAD advises a medicated cleanser once or twice a month, especially during warm and humid periods, to prevent regrowth. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

travel-medicine-guide.question: What prescriptions do I need before international travel?
travel-medicine-guide.answerHtml: A pre-travel medicine visit addresses four core pharmacological prevention needs per the CDC Yellow Book pre-travel consultation guidelines: (1) malaria prophylaxis: atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) or doxycycline for chloroquine-resistant destinations; (2) traveler's diarrhea standby: azithromycin (preferred over ciprofloxacin for South/Southeast Asia due to fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter); (3) altitude sickness prevention: acetazolamide 125 mg BID for moderate-altitude destinations per the CDC Yellow Book altitude guidelines; and (4) motion sickness prevention. Yellow fever vaccines, primaquine, and tafenoquine require an in-person travel clinic. All prescriptions are non-controlled; self-pay option starts at $79.

tretinoin-guide.question: What is the best treatment for photoaging and wrinkles in 2026?
tretinoin-guide.answerHtml: For adults seeking evidence-based prevention and treatment of photoaging (sun-induced wrinkles, uneven pigmentation, and rough texture), two well-supported steps are daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen and prescription tretinoin. The FDA approved topical tretinoin for acne in 1971 and for the palliative treatment of photoaging in 1995; tazarotene 0.1% cream is also FDA-labeled for fine facial wrinkling. A 2022 systematic review of 7 randomized controlled trials found tretinoin improved wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines, with improvement significant after 4 months and continuing over 24 months. In a 48-week trial, tretinoin 0.025% and 0.1% produced similar improvement, with significantly more irritation at 0.1%. Adapalene 0.3% gel was non-inferior to tretinoin 0.05% cream for photoaging (Bagatin 2018). The tretinoin label for photoaging says it should not be used during pregnancy. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can prescribe tretinoin after reviewing skin type, medical history, and photoprotection habits.

truck-driver-health-risks-telehealth.question: What are the biggest health risks for truck drivers and how can telehealth help?
truck-driver-health-risks-telehealth.answerHtml: Truck drivers carry a heavy chronic disease burden. In NIOSH's national survey of 1,670 long-haul truck drivers, 69% were obese (vs 31% of U.S. working adults), 14.4% reported diabetes (vs 6.8%), and 61% reported two or more risk factors such as hypertension, smoking or short sleep (Sieber et al., 2014). A 2024 BMC Public Health meta-analysis estimated that 61.75% of truck drivers have musculoskeletal disorders (Tahernejad et al., 2024). In a sample of 107 Canadian long-haul drivers, 44% reported depressive symptoms in the past year, and 80% of them had no professional mental health treatment (Crizzle et al., 2020). An FMCSA-sponsored study found that almost one-third (28%) of commercial truck drivers have mild to severe sleep apnea (FMCSA). Telehealth removes the structural barriers: no clinic, no time off route, prescriptions sent to any pharmacy on your route. DOT physicals require an in-person certified Medical Examiner and cannot be completed via telehealth. A licensed clinician, accessible via telehealth or in-person care, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

type-2-diabetes-medication-guide.question: What medications are used to manage type 2 diabetes?
type-2-diabetes-medication-guide.answerHtml: The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend choosing type 2 diabetes medicines for heart and kidney protection as well as blood sugar. For adults with established or high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, a GLP-1 receptor agonist (such as semaglutide) and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor (such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin) is recommended irrespective of A1C; an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended for heart failure, and an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA for chronic kidney disease. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe GLP-1 medications, such as semaglutide or tirzepatide, for diabetes. In the SURPASS-2 trial, tirzepatide lowered A1C more than semaglutide 1 mg, with greater weight loss; in a manufacturer-funded real-world study, patients new to GLP-1 therapy who started tirzepatide had a mean A1C reduction of 1.3% and 10.2 kg weight loss at 12 months versus 0.9% and 6.1 kg for semaglutide. Metformin historically has been the first-line treatment and remains common when glucose lowering is the main need. An A1C goal below 7% is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults, with less stringent goals for some, such as people with complex health or limited life expectancy. DKA (fruity breath, vomiting, fast deep breathing) and severe hypoglycemia (a low with confusion, or one that needs another person's help) require emergency care. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

urinary-tract-infection-uti-guide.question: What are UTI symptoms, causes, and treatments?
urinary-tract-infection-uti-guide.answerHtml: UTIs are among the most common bacterial infections, accounting for 0.9% of U.S. ambulatory care visits (Foxman, 2014), and most cases of cystitis are caused by E. coli. Combinations such as painful urination plus frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation raise the probability of a UTI to more than 90% (Bent et al., JAMA 2002). For acute uncomplicated cystitis in healthy, non-pregnant, premenopausal women, nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX (where local resistance is under 20%) and fosfomycin are appropriate first-line agents, and fluoroquinolones should be reserved for when other agents are not appropriate (CDC). Typical regimens are nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, TMP-SMX 160/800 mg twice daily for 3 days, or fosfomycin 3 g as a single dose (EAU guideline). For recurrent UTIs, the 2025 AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline update expands non-antibiotic prevention options; the European guideline recommends vaginal estrogen after menopause and methenamine hippurate, with antibiotic prophylaxis when non-antimicrobial measures have failed. Fever, flank pain, or vomiting suggest a kidney infection and need prompt in-person care. Most uncomplicated cases are appropriate for telehealth evaluation; complicated or red-flag presentations should be seen in person.

us-pharmacy-guide-for-international-visi.question: How does an international visitor pick up a prescription at a US pharmacy?
us-pharmacy-guide-for-international-visi.answerHtml: US pharmacies dispense prescription drugs on the prescription of a practitioner licensed by law, so a visitor whose prescription is only from a home-country doctor should plan on a new one from a US-licensed clinician. Which photo ID a pharmacy accepts at pickup depends on the state and the pharmacy. North Carolina's law, for example, requires a driver's license, state ID card, military ID or passport before a Schedule II controlled substance is dispensed, and the state pharmacy board says the passport need not be US-issued; national IDs such as India's Aadhaar or Mexico's INE are not on that list, so carry a passport. Discount services such as GoodRx and SingleCare are free and are not insurance; SingleCare says its coupons cannot be combined with insurance. Federal law requires pharmacists to offer counseling to Medicaid patients, and most states extended counseling to all patients, so ask the pharmacist to explain the medicine before leaving the counter. For visitors booking through TeleDirectMD, the platform accepts a passport or any government-issued photo ID; workplace and student IDs are excluded.

vaginal-dryness-treatment-guide.question: How do you treat vaginal dryness and genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)?
vaginal-dryness-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) affects approximately 27% to 84% of postmenopausal women and is likely underdiagnosed and undertreated, per the 2020 NAMS Position Statement. Nonprescription vaginal moisturizers and lubricants give sufficient relief for most women with mild symptoms. For moderate to severe symptoms, NAMS lists low-dose vaginal estrogen, vaginal DHEA (prasterone), systemic estrogen therapy, and ospemifene as effective treatments; ospemifene is taken as one 60 mg tablet with food once daily per its FDA label. For women with a history of breast cancer, ACOG recommends nonhormonal treatment first and says low-dose vaginal estrogen may be used if that has not helped, after discussing risks and benefits; NAMS notes that safety data in breast cancer are insufficient. NAMS also found too few placebo-controlled trials of vaginal laser to recommend it. A licensed clinician, by telehealth or in person, can review the symptoms and prescribe appropriate therapy.

visby-at-home-sti-pcr-test-review.question: Is the Visby at-home PCR test for STIs accurate and how do you use the results?
visby-at-home-sti-pcr-test-review.answerHtml: The Visby Medical Women's Sexual Health Test received FDA marketing authorization on March 28, 2025 as the first test for chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomoniasis that can be bought without a prescription and performed entirely at home. It is a single-use PCR test run on a self-collected vaginal swab, with results in about 30 minutes. In the FDA-reviewed study, it correctly identified 97.2% of positive chlamydia, 100% of positive gonorrhea, and 97.8% of positive trichomoniasis samples, and 98.5% to 99.1% of negative samples. A study from the test's maker, published as an abstract in Open Forum Infectious Diseases (January 2025), reported at least 95.0% sensitivity and 98.0% specificity for each organism. A positive result needs clinician follow-up, so do not self-treat. Under the CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines, chlamydia is treated with doxycycline and first-line gonorrhea treatment is a ceftriaxone injection. A negative result does not rule out HIV, syphilis, herpes, or HPV. A licensed clinician, through telehealth or in-person evaluation, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend next steps.

wildfire-smoke-health-guide.question: How do I protect my health from wildfire smoke?
wildfire-smoke-health-guide.answerHtml: Wildfire smoke exposure is largely a fine-particle (PM2.5) problem, and studies suggest wildfire PM2.5 is more harmful than the same amount from other sources: in one Southern California study, respiratory hospitalizations rose 1.3 to up to 10 percent per 10 micrograms per cubic meter of wildfire PM2.5, versus 0.67 to 1.3 percent for other PM2.5 (Aguilera et al., Nature Communications 2021). Check AirNow: at AQI 101 to 150 (Orange), members of sensitive groups, including people with heart or lung disease, older adults, children and teenagers, and outdoor workers, may experience health effects, and EPA advises them to make outdoor activities shorter and less intense; at 151 (Red), some of the general public may be affected. Stay inside with windows and doors closed, and set up a clean room with a portable air cleaner sized for the room. In EPA testing, a DIY Corsi-Rosenthal box (a box fan with four MERV 13 filters and a cardboard shroud) delivered about 401 cubic feet per minute of clean air, and EPA researchers found such designs more effective than higher-priced commercial units. If you must go outdoors, CDC advises a NIOSH Approved N95 respirator; dust masks, surgical masks, bandanas, and wet cloths will not protect against smoke. If you have heart disease, contact your healthcare provider for palpitations, unusual fatigue, or shortness of breath. Call 911 or go to the ER for severe trouble breathing, chest pain, or a possible heart attack or stroke.

yeast-infection-guide.question: What is the best treatment for a yeast infection in 2026?
yeast-infection-guide.answerHtml: A vaginal yeast infection (vulvovaginal candidiasis, or VVC) affects an estimated 75 percent of women at least once in their lifetime and is usually caused by Candida albicans.[1] First-line treatment in the CDC 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines is a short course of an azole antifungal, either a single 150 mg oral dose of fluconazole or an over-the-counter or prescription vaginal azole such as miconazole, clotrimazole, or terconazole; azoles relieve symptoms and clear cultures in 80 to 90 percent of patients who complete therapy.[1] Fewer than 5 percent of women develop recurrent infection (three or more episodes in less than a year, by the CDC definition), which is managed with longer suppression using weekly fluconazole, as in the landmark Sobel NEJM trial.[1] Newer prescription agents, ibrexafungerp and oteseconazole, are contraindicated in pregnancy, and oteseconazole is approved only for women who are not of reproductive potential.[25][26] Self-diagnosis is unreliable: in one study, fewer than 35 percent of women who assumed they had a yeast infection actually did.[5] A licensed clinician, in person or via telehealth, can confirm the diagnosis and recommend the right treatment.

flu-season-guide.question: When is flu season in the United States?
flu-season-guide.answerHtml: In the United States, flu season usually occurs in the fall and winter, with activity most often peaking between December and February, according to the CDC. The CDC recommends that everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine each season, ideally by the end of October, and vaccination can still be beneficial as long as flu viruses are circulating. In seasons when the vaccine viruses are similar to those spreading, studies show flu vaccination reduced the risk of a flu-related doctor's visit by 40% to 60%. The flu shot cannot cause the flu; common side effects such as soreness where the shot was given and a low-grade fever usually last 1 to 2 days. Because flu and COVID-19 share many symptoms, testing is needed to tell them apart.

flu-shot-side-effects-guide.question: What are the most common flu shot side effects?
flu-shot-side-effects-guide.answerHtml: The most common flu shot side effects are soreness, redness, tenderness, or swelling where the shot was given, according to the CDC. Headache, fever, muscle aches, nausea, and fatigue can also occur, and side effects are generally mild and go away on their own within a few days (CDC key facts; CDC flu vaccine safety). The flu shot cannot cause the flu, because it is made with inactivated (killed) virus or a single protein from a flu virus. Life-threatening allergic reactions are rare, and if flu vaccination adds any risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome, the CDC estimates it is small, on the order of one to two additional cases per million doses.

flu-test-guide.question: What is a flu test and how is flu diagnosed?
flu-test-guide.answerHtml: A flu test detects influenza virus in a nasal or throat swab. The two main types are rapid antigen tests and molecular tests. Rapid antigen tests give results in about 10 to 15 minutes but have only low to moderate sensitivity, roughly 50% to 70%, so a negative result does not rule out flu. Rapid molecular assays have 90% to 95% sensitivity, and laboratory RT-PCR has very high sensitivity and specificity. For outpatients, the IDSA recommends rapid molecular assays over rapid antigen tests. FDA-authorized at-home tests that check for both flu and COVID-19 are available. Most are antigen tests, so a negative result can be wrong.

flu-treatment-guide.question: What should an adult do for flu within and after the first 48 hours?
flu-treatment-guide.answerHtml: For adults with flu symptoms, the first decision is severity and complication risk, not simply which medicine to buy. CDC and the IDSA guideline prioritize prompt antiviral treatment for hospitalized, severely ill, progressively worsening or higher-risk patients; a clinician may recommend treatment even after 48 hours and should not always wait for a positive test. In otherwise healthy adults with uncomplicated illness, early antivirals can modestly shorten symptoms, but a guaranteed cure or prevention of hospitalization should not be promised. Standard adult oseltamivir treatment is usually twice daily for five days, with kidney-function adjustments when needed; baloxavir is a single weight-based dose for eligible uncomplicated cases within its labeled window. OTC medicines relieve symptoms rather than treat influenza virus. Breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion, not urinating, or improvement followed by deterioration needs urgent assessment.

tooth-infection-antibiotics-guide.question: What is the best antibiotic for a tooth infection?
tooth-infection-antibiotics-guide.answerHtml: For an adult with a tooth abscess that is causing systemic involvement (such as fever, malaise, or spread into the fascial spaces or local lymph nodes), the ADA 2019 clinical practice guideline (Lockhart et al., JADA) suggests amoxicillin 500 mg by mouth three times a day, or penicillin VK 500 mg four times a day, for 3 to 7 days, together with urgent definitive dental treatment or an urgent dental referral. For a penicillin allergy without a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or hives, it suggests cephalexin; with that history, it lists azithromycin or clindamycin 300 mg four times a day. Clindamycin carries an FDA Black Box warning for C. difficile infection, and the guideline notes that about 10% of people report a penicillin allergy while less than 1% are truly allergic. Antibiotics are not a substitute for dental care: the guideline says immediate definitive dental treatment should be prioritized in all cases.

does-azo-treat-a-uti-guide.question: Does AZO treat or cure a UTI?
does-azo-treat-a-uti-guide.answerHtml: No. AZO (phenazopyridine) is a urinary tract analgesic, not an antibiotic. It relieves urinary pain, burning, urgency, and frequency, but it does not cure the infection. Antibiotics are what treat a UTI. Phenazopyridine turns urine reddish-orange and can interfere with laboratory tests, including urine tests, so tell a clinician you have taken it before testing. The over-the-counter label says not to use it for more than 2 days without consulting a doctor, and it is not a substitute for medical care.

uti-symptoms-in-women-guide.question: What are the first signs of a UTI in women?
uti-symptoms-in-women-guide.answerHtml: The earliest signs are usually burning or pain with urination (dysuria), a sudden and strong need to urinate (urgency), and urinating more often than usual (frequency). In women with urinary symptoms, painful urination plus frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation raises the probability of a bladder infection to more than 90%, per the Bent 2002 JAMA review. Some women also notice cloudy, bloody, or strong-smelling urine, or pressure or discomfort in the lower abdomen. Itching, a thick white discharge, or a fishy odor points away from a UTI and toward a yeast infection or bacterial vaginosis instead. If you are pregnant, contact your OB or an in-person clinician promptly; UTIs in pregnancy need different evaluation.

burning-when-you-pee-guide.question: What causes burning when you pee?
burning-when-you-pee-guide.answerHtml: Burning or painful urination, called dysuria, most often comes from a urinary tract infection (UTI), but it can also be caused by a yeast infection, a sexually transmitted infection (STI), interstitial cystitis, a kidney stone, or chemical irritants. The pattern of symptoms points to the cause. Burning felt inside with urinary frequency and urgency, without vaginal discharge or irritation, suggests a bladder infection. Burning felt when urine touches irritated external tissue, with itching and a thick, curdy discharge, suggests a yeast infection. Burning with urethral discharge and a new partner suggests an STI such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Because the treatments differ, the cause should be identified rather than assumed. Seek urgent care for fever, flank pain, nausea, or vomiting, and get prompt evaluation if you are pregnant.

uti-emergency-warning-signs-guide.question: What are the warning signs a UTI has reached the kidneys?
uti-emergency-warning-signs-guide.answerHtml: A UTI has likely reached the kidneys when fever, chills, flank or back pain, nausea or vomiting, and a feeling of being systemically unwell join the usual urinary symptoms. Those are the classic signs of a kidney infection (pyelonephritis), and they call for prompt medical evaluation. The 2025 IDSA guideline on complicated UTI states that systemic signs such as fever suggest the infection has extended beyond the bladder, and it classifies pyelonephritis as a complicated UTI. Seek urgent or emergency care for those symptoms regardless of what a home dipstick shows, because a urine strip detects markers of inflammation and bacteria but cannot tell whether an infection is confined to the bladder or has moved into the kidneys. Pregnancy, immune suppression, older age, and inability to keep fluids down all lower the threshold for urgent assessment.

impetigo-guide.question: What is the best treatment for impetigo?
impetigo-guide.answerHtml: The best treatment depends on how much skin is involved. For mild impetigo in adults or children, bullous or nonbullous, a topical antibiotic such as mupirocin 2% or retapamulin 1% twice daily for 5 days is first line, and a Cochrane review found topical mupirocin as effective as, or more effective than, oral antibiotics. For numerous lesions, outbreaks, ecthyma, or impetigo that does not respond to a topical antibiotic within 3 to 5 days, oral antibiotics such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin are recommended, with doxycycline, clindamycin, or TMP-SMX when MRSA is suspected or confirmed. Antibiotic treatment also limits spread to others. A licensed clinician can confirm the diagnosis and prescribe appropriate therapy, in person or via telehealth.

melasma-guide.question: What is the best treatment for melasma?
melasma-guide.answerHtml: The foundation of melasma treatment is daily sun protection: dermatologists often recommend a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher containing zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and iron oxide. On top of that, hydroquinone alone and triple combination cream (hydroquinone, tretinoin, and a corticosteroid) are the most effective, best-studied topicals. Over-the-counter hydroquinone products can no longer be legally sold in the U.S., so hydroquinone is used by prescription. Oral tranexamic acid is an off-label add-on for moderate to severe or recurrent melasma, with meta-analytic evidence of added benefit with triple cream, but its U.S. label rules it out for people with a history of blood clots or who use combined hormonal birth control. Melasma is chronic and tends to return with unprotected sun exposure, so sun protection is lifelong. Visible results usually take 3 to 12 months. A clinician can confirm the diagnosis and build a plan appropriate to your skin tone and triggers.

perioral-dermatitis-guide.question: What is the best treatment for perioral dermatitis?
perioral-dermatitis-guide.answerHtml: The first and most important step is stopping all facial corticosteroids and products, often called zero therapy, because steroid use is the most common association. The rash may flare as a steroid cream is withdrawn, so tapering matters. For more severe or stubborn cases, oral tetracycline is the best-supported first-line medicine, and topical options such as metronidazole, erythromycin, or pimecrolimus are used for moderate disease, although the overall evidence is low or very low certainty. Treatment usually runs 4 to 8 weeks, and recurrence can occur if treatment is too short. A clinician can confirm the diagnosis and distinguish it from rosacea or acne.

trichomoniasis-guide.question: What is the best treatment for trichomoniasis?
trichomoniasis-guide.answerHtml: Trichomoniasis is treated with a nitroimidazole antibiotic: the CDC recommends metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days for women, a single 2 g dose of metronidazole for men, or tinidazole 2 g as a single dose as an alternative for either. Treating all sex partners at the same time is vital, since most repeat infections likely come from reinfection. People should abstain from sex until everyone is treated and any symptoms resolve. Sexually active women are retested about 3 months later. A licensed clinician can confirm the diagnosis with a highly sensitive test and prescribe the right regimen.

hydroquinone-guide.question: What is hydroquinone and how does it work?
hydroquinone-guide.answerHtml: Hydroquinone is a topical medicine that lightens dark patches by inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in making melanin. Alone or in a triple combination cream, it is among the most effective and best-studied treatments for melasma. In the United States it is prescription-only: since the CARES Act took effect on September 23, 2020, over-the-counter hydroquinone skin lighteners need FDA approval before they can be sold. Used appropriately under medical supervision and within recommended concentrations, it is considered safe and effective. The main long-term risk is exogenous ochronosis, a blue-black skin darkening linked to long-term excessive use that may be permanent, which is why it is used for limited courses rather than indefinitely. A clinician can confirm the diagnosis and build a plan that pairs hydroquinone with daily sun protection.

topical-steroid-withdrawal-guide.question: What is topical steroid withdrawal and how is it treated?
topical-steroid-withdrawal-guide.answerHtml: Topical steroid withdrawal, sometimes called red skin syndrome or steroid addiction, is a skin reaction reported after stopping a topical corticosteroid that was used frequently or continually for a long time, usually a moderate to high potency steroid. Typical features are burning, redness that can spread beyond the treated area, and a flare worse than the original condition. The UK medicines regulator understands severe reactions to be very infrequent, and a systematic review rated the evidence as low quality. Treatment is not well studied: supervised gradual tapering, moisturizing, and managing itch, pain and infection are commonly recommended, though some clinicians who treat the condition report little difference between tapering and stopping at once. Any change to a prescribed steroid should be planned with a clinician rather than driven by fear. A clinician can distinguish a true withdrawal reaction from the underlying skin condition and build a safe plan.

metronidazole-guide.question: What is metronidazole and what is it used for?
metronidazole-guide.answerHtml: Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial that treats certain anaerobic bacteria and protozoa. CDC recommends it for the sexually transmitted infection trichomoniasis and for bacterial vaginosis, and it is also used for certain dental, abdominal, and parasitic infections. Complete the full course even if you feel better. The FDA label says to avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least three days after, while the 2021 CDC guideline says refraining from alcohol is unnecessary, so ask your prescriber which advice to follow. A licensed clinician determines whether metronidazole is the right drug and the correct dose for the specific infection.

bv-vs-yeast-infection-guide.question: How do I tell a bacterial vaginosis from a yeast infection?
bv-vs-yeast-infection-guide.answerHtml: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) and a yeast infection (vulvovaginal candidiasis) can look alike but have different causes: BV is an overgrowth of certain vaginal bacteria that a healthcare provider treats with antibiotics, while a yeast infection is usually caused by Candida albicans and is treated with antifungals. Vaginal pH is a useful clue: a pH above 4.5 is one of the CDC criteria for diagnosing BV, while yeast is associated with a normal pH below 4.5, though pH alone is not specific. BV typically causes a thin white or gray discharge with a fishy odor, while yeast typically causes itching, soreness and a thick, curdy discharge, but no single symptom settles it. BV is common: it was found in 29.2 percent of U.S. women aged 14 to 49 in a national survey, and most had no symptoms. Getting it right matters because the treatments differ: the over-the-counter vaginal products CDC lists for yeast are antifungals, while BV is treated with prescribed antibiotics. A clinician can confirm which one it is with a pH check and a swab, which is more reliable than guessing from symptoms alone.

bv-discharge-guide.question: What does bacterial vaginosis discharge look like?
bv-discharge-guide.answerHtml: Bacterial vaginosis classically causes a thin, milklike discharge that smoothly coats the vaginal walls, usually white or gray, often with a strong fish-like odor, especially after sex. That discharge is one of the four Amsel criteria that CDC describes for diagnosis, along with a vaginal pH above 4.5, clue cells on microscopy and a fishy odor on the whiff test; at least three are needed. The texture is a useful contrast with yeast, which tends to cause thick, curdy discharge, and with trichomoniasis, whose discharge can be diffuse, malodorous or yellow-green. A critical caveat: most BV has no symptoms at all, with 84 percent of women with BV in a national survey reporting none, so discharge alone is not a reliable rule-in and its absence is not a rule-out. Because a medical history alone is not enough to tell the causes of vaginal symptoms apart, a swab test rather than a visual guess is the reliable way to identify which one you have.

bv-smell-guide.question: Why does bacterial vaginosis cause a fishy smell?
bv-smell-guide.answerHtml: The fishy odor of bacterial vaginosis comes from amines. In BV, the normal lactobacilli are replaced by an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria, and vaginal fluid contains amines such as putrescine, cadaverine and trimethylamine. Trimethylamine, which bacteria make from trimethylamine oxide, is the compound linked to the fishy smell, and adding an alkali releases it. That is the basis of the whiff test, one of the four Amsel criteria in the CDC 2021 STI guidelines. Semen neutralizes vaginal acidity, which helps explain why CDC describes the odor as strong especially after sex. The odor is not a hygiene failure, and douching does not fix it: CDC says no data support douching for treatment or symptom relief and that it might increase the risk of relapse. The odor resolves when BV itself is treated with a prescription antibiotic regimen, such as oral metronidazole, metronidazole gel or clindamycin cream, not with deodorizing products.

boric-acid-for-bv-guide.question: Does boric acid treat bacterial vaginosis?
boric-acid-for-bv-guide.answerHtml: Boric acid is not a first-line treatment for bacterial vaginosis and is not an FDA-approved drug. CDC's 2021 STI treatment guidelines list it only as a limited-data option for women with multiple recurrences: an oral nitroimidazole for 7 days, followed by intravaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days and suppressive 0.75% metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4 to 6 months. That approach comes from a retrospective chart review by Reichman and colleagues of 58 women, in which cure after the antibiotic and boric acid phases ranged from 88 to 92 percent at 7 and 12 weeks. Cumulative cure, which included maintenance metronidazole gel for women in remission, was 87, 78, and 65 percent at 12, 16, and 28 weeks. A 2021 safety review concluded that vaginal boric acid appears safe at commonly prescribed doses, noted that safety data are sparse, and found the data insufficient to change guidance that it be avoided in pregnancy. Because it is used off-label, it should be used under a clinician's direction, not self-prescribed.

how-to-get-rid-of-bv-guide.question: How do you get rid of bacterial vaginosis for good?
how-to-get-rid-of-bv-guide.answerHtml: Getting rid of BV is a two-part problem: clearing the current episode and stopping it from coming back. For the first part, the CDC's recommended regimens are metronidazole 500 mg by mouth twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole 0.75% gel once daily for 5 days, or clindamycin 2% cream at bedtime for 7 days, with single-dose secnidazole, tinidazole and other clindamycin forms as alternatives. In one trial of 7-day oral treatment, cure was 76.8 percent at 14 days and 64.5 percent at 1 month. The second part is harder: in one cohort, 58 percent of women had BV again within 12 months of oral metronidazole. For multiple recurrences, twice-weekly metronidazole gel cut recurrence to 25.5 percent versus 59.1 percent on placebo during 16 weeks of use, though the benefit fades after it stops. Treating a male partner reduced recurrence from 63 to 35 percent at 12 weeks in a 2025 trial of monogamous couples, which is newer than CDC guidance that does not recommend routine partner treatment. Boric acid is part of a limited-data CDC option for multiple recurrences, and the Lactin-V probiotic is not yet FDA cleared. A clinician can confirm the diagnosis and build the plan that fits your recurrence pattern.

vaginal-yeast-infection-guide.question: What are the symptoms and causes of a vaginal yeast infection?
vaginal-yeast-infection-guide.answerHtml: A vaginal yeast infection (vulvovaginal candidiasis) typically causes vulvar itching, vaginal soreness, burning when urine touches irritated skin, pain with sex, and a thick, curd-like discharge.[1] It is caused by overgrowth of Candida, usually Candida albicans,[8] and an estimated 75 percent of women have at least one episode.[1] Recognized triggers include antibiotics, poorly controlled diabetes, pregnancy and other high-estrogen states, and immune suppression.[7] Because none of these symptoms is specific, a reliable diagnosis combines the symptom pattern with a vaginal pH reading and microscopy or culture,[1] and in one study only about a third of women who self-diagnosed a yeast infection actually had one.[5] Most uncomplicated infections respond to a short course of an azole antifungal, either a single 150 mg oral fluconazole dose or a topical cream or suppository, which relieves symptoms in 80 to 90 percent of patients who complete treatment.[1]

yeast-infection-vs-bv-guide.question: How do I tell a yeast infection from BV?
yeast-infection-vs-bv-guide.answerHtml: Yeast infection and bacterial vaginosis (BV) are, along with trichomoniasis, the infections most often behind vaginal symptoms, and they are easy to confuse because both can cause discharge and discomfort, yet they are treated with entirely different medicines. A yeast infection is an overgrowth of Candida that typically causes itching, soreness and a thick, curdy discharge, while BV is a bacterial imbalance in which a thin, milky discharge and a fishy odor are among the diagnostic signs.[1] Vaginal pH is a quick objective clue: a yeast infection is associated with a normal pH below 4.5, while a pH above 4.5 is common with BV or trichomoniasis.[1] In one study, only about a third of women who self-diagnosed a yeast infection had a yeast infection alone,[4] so confirming the cause with pH testing and microscopy before treating matters.[1] Yeast is treated with azole antifungals (oral fluconazole, or topical clotrimazole or miconazole), while BV is treated with antibiotics (metronidazole or clindamycin).[1]

fluconazole-for-yeast-infection-guide.question: Is one fluconazole pill enough for a yeast infection?
fluconazole-for-yeast-infection-guide.answerHtml: For most uncomplicated vaginal yeast infections, yes. CDC's 2021 treatment guidelines list fluconazole (Diflucan) 150 mg as a single oral dose, and azole treatment relieves symptoms and clears cultures in 80 to 90 percent of people who complete therapy.[2] Severe infections are treated with two 150 mg doses taken 72 hours apart or 7 to 14 days of a topical azole, and in pregnancy CDC recommends only 7-day topical azoles.[2] In a 2025 network meta-analysis of 50 randomized trials, every oral and topical treatment studied was highly effective compared with placebo (over 75 percent), and single-dose fluconazole was slightly more effective than multiple-day topical therapy for early clinical cure.[6] Because it is taken by mouth it can interact with other medicines, and the FDA label says use in pregnancy should be avoided except for severe or potentially life-threatening fungal infections.[1] When an infection persists or returns despite fluconazole, fluconazole-resistant Candida or a non-albicans species may be responsible, and alternative treatments exist.[8]

recurrent-yeast-infection-guide.question: What is the best treatment for recurrent yeast infections in 2026?
recurrent-yeast-infection-guide.answerHtml: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis means repeated symptomatic yeast infections within a year: three or more by CDC's definition, or four or more in many studies. A systematic review estimated it affects about 138 million women worldwide each year.[11][2] The evidence-based cornerstone is induction treatment to clear the current episode followed by maintenance suppression, classically oral fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for six months. In the landmark Sobel trial, 90.8 percent of women on weekly fluconazole stayed disease-free at six months versus 35.9 percent on placebo.[1] The FDA has also approved two newer oral options to reduce recurrences: oteseconazole (Vivjoa), which cut recurrence to roughly 5 percent through 48 weeks but is approved only for women who are not of reproductive potential, and ibrexafungerp (Brexafemme), taken on one day each month for six months, which is contraindicated in pregnancy.[5][6][14][15] Because recurrence can be linked to diabetes, antibiotic use, a resistant or non-albicans strain, or a different condition that mimics yeast, reversible causes should be looked for rather than only suppressing symptoms.[13]

yeast-infection-home-remedies-guide.question: Do home remedies actually work for a yeast infection?
yeast-infection-home-remedies-guide.answerHtml: Most home remedies for yeast infection have little or no evidence behind them, and a few can cause real harm, but one genuine exception stands out: boric acid vaginal capsules, which have clinical evidence for recurrent infection when standard treatment fails because of non-albicans or azole-resistant yeast.[1] By contrast, garlic and tea tree oil have shown laboratory activity without the clinical studies needed to recommend them,[10] and fresh raw garlic used on the body can cause severe irritation and chemical burns.[12] Probiotics taken alongside antifungal treatment may improve short-term cure, but the evidence is low or very low quality and showed no long-term benefit.[2] The most important caution is diagnostic: in one study, only about a third of women who bought an over-the-counter antifungal for a self-diagnosed yeast infection actually had one, so the single best 'home' step is to confirm the diagnosis before using any remedy, including the over-the-counter antifungals that genuinely work for uncomplicated cases.[5]

cold-sore-stages-guide.question: What are the five stages of a cold sore?
cold-sore-stages-guide.answerHtml: A cold sore usually starts with a tingling, itching, or burning feeling; over the next 48 hours one or more blisters appear, then burst and crust over into a scab before the skin heals, according to the NHS. This guide groups that sequence into five stages: (1) tingling or prodrome, (2) blistering, (3) weeping, (4) crusting or scabbing, and (5) healing. For many people a cold sore goes away without treatment in 7 to 14 days, according to the American Academy of Dermatology. The tingle is the stage that matters most for treatment: the valacyclovir (Valtrex) label says therapy should start at the earliest symptom, such as tingling, itching, or burning, and that its efficacy when started after a bump, blister, or ulcer has formed has not been established. Cold sores are contagious from the first tingle until they have completely healed.

how-to-get-rid-of-cold-sore-fast-guide.question: What is the fastest way to get rid of a cold sore?
how-to-get-rid-of-cold-sore-fast-guide.answerHtml: The fastest, best-evidenced way to shorten a cold sore is to start an oral antiviral at the very first sign, the tingle or itching of the prodrome, rather than waiting for the blister to form. A one-day course of valacyclovir (2 grams twice, 12 hours apart) reduced the median episode length by about a day in the pivotal trials, and single-dose famciclovir (1,500 mg) shortened healing by about two days in its own trial. Over-the-counter docosanol cream shortened healing by about 18 hours in its main trial, and a review rates oral antivirals above topical treatment for episodic use. Home care such as ice in a washcloth or a warm washcloth and an over-the-counter pain reliever eases discomfort, per MedlinePlus, but it does not cure the sore. The single most powerful move is timing: treat at the tingle, not after the fact.

cold-sore-vs-pimple-guide.question: How can you tell a cold sore from a pimple?
cold-sore-vs-pimple-guide.answerHtml: A cold sore and a pimple can look alike at a glance, but they are different problems. A cold sore is usually caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It often starts with tingling, itching or burning, then forms small fluid-filled blisters that break open, leak and crust as they heal, and it is contagious. For many people it goes away without treatment in 7 to 14 days. A pimple forms when a pore becomes clogged with oil and skin cells and then inflamed; it may have a white or yellow center, and acne is not contagious. A warning tingle and small blisters that later crust point to a cold sore. These features are described by MedlinePlus on oral herpes and acne and by the American Academy of Dermatology. Because the causes differ, the treatments differ: cold sores are treated with antiviral medicine, while pimples are treated with acne care.

cold-sore-inside-mouth-guide.question: What causes cold sores inside the mouth, and how are they different from canker sores?
cold-sore-inside-mouth-guide.answerHtml: Sores inside the mouth caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1) occur in two main settings: a first, or primary, infection, most common in children between 6 months and 5 years old, which can cause fever and painful sores across the gums and mouth (herpetic gingivostomatitis), and recurrent outbreaks, which most often affect the firmly attached tissue of the gums and the roof of the mouth, although the inner lip can also be involved. A canker sore (aphthous ulcer) is different: it has not been linked to herpes simplex virus, is not contagious, and is typically a round, shallow ulcer with a red rim on the loose lining of the inner cheek or lip. These distinctions are described in a systematic review of primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, a case series and review of oral HSV-1, a case series of recurrent intraoral HSV-1, and a review of recurrent aphthous stomatitis. Because the causes differ, so does treatment: antiviral medication can speed healing of herpes sores, while antivirals are neither necessary nor effective for canker sores, which are managed with symptom relief.

valacyclovir-for-cold-sores-guide.question: What is the valacyclovir dose for a cold sore, and how well does it work?
valacyclovir-for-cold-sores-guide.answerHtml: For a cold sore, the FDA-labeled valacyclovir (brand Valtrex) dose is 2 grams twice in one day, taken 12 hours apart, started at the earliest symptom such as tingling, itching, or burning, as stated in the current FDA label and tested in the randomized trials by Spruance and colleagues. Valacyclovir is converted in the body to acyclovir: about 54 percent of a dose reaches the bloodstream as acyclovir, compared with an average of 10 to 20 percent for oral acyclovir itself, according to the FDA labels for valacyclovir and acyclovir. In the trials, people started treatment at the first symptoms, before any visible sore, and the median episode was 1.0 day shorter than with placebo, with faster healing and pain relief. The label states that benefit when treatment starts after a bump, blister, or ulcer has appeared has not been established.

gout-diet-foods-to-avoid-guide.question: What foods cause gout and which should you avoid?
gout-diet-foods-to-avoid-guide.answerHtml: Diet alone rarely controls gout, but certain foods and drinks are repeatedly tied to a higher risk. In large prospective studies of men, the strongest dietary associations were sugar-sweetened soda (relative risk 1.85 for two or more a day), high seafood intake (relative risk 1.51), beer (relative risk 1.49 per daily 12-ounce serving), and high meat intake (relative risk 1.41), per the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, the fructose cohort, and the alcohol cohort. Higher dairy intake (relative risk 0.56), coffee, and a DASH-style eating pattern were associated with lower risk, while purine-rich vegetables were not linked to gout. The 2020 ACR guideline conditionally recommends limiting alcohol, purine-rich food, and high-fructose corn syrup, plus weight loss for people who are overweight, while stressing that diet is an add-on to treat-to-target urate lowering when that therapy is indicated.

gout-attack-treatment-guide.question: What is the fastest way to treat a gout attack?
gout-attack-treatment-guide.answerHtml: Start an anti-inflammatory as early as possible, ideally within 24 hours of the first symptoms. The 2020 ACR guideline lists three first-line options and does not rank them, leaving the choice to the person's other conditions, such as kidney disease, ulcer or bleeding risk, heart failure or diabetes, and their other medicines: low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg one hour later), a full dose of an NSAID, or a short course of an oral corticosteroid such as prednisone. In the AGREE trial, low-dose colchicine matched high-dose colchicine for pain relief at 24 hours (37.8 percent versus 32.7 percent with at least 50 percent pain reduction) with far fewer digestive side effects. In a separate double-blind trial, prednisolone and naproxen were equally effective over four days. Keep taking any long-term urate-lowering medicine such as allopurinol during the attack, use ice as an add-on, and get prompt in-person care for a first-ever hot, swollen joint or a swollen joint with fever.

allopurinol-vs-colchicine-guide.question: What is the difference between allopurinol and colchicine?
allopurinol-vs-colchicine-guide.answerHtml: These two drugs do different jobs. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that lowers serum urate over weeks to months and is the preferred long-term, preventive medicine for gout. Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory that treats an active flare and can provide short-term prophylaxis when urate-lowering therapy is started. Allopurinol is not a flare treatment, and colchicine is not a urate-lowering drug, so the two are not interchangeable. In practice they are often paired: a person starts allopurinol at a low dose, titrated to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL, while colchicine (or an NSAID), usually for at least 3 to 6 months, helps prevent the flares that can occur as urate falls. The 2020 ACR guideline makes allopurinol the preferred first urate-lowering drug and colchicine or an NSAID the recommended flare prophylaxis.

uric-acid-levels-guide.question: What is a normal uric acid level, and what is considered high?
uric-acid-levels-guide.answerHtml: Serum urate (uric acid) is usually reported in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). Normal ranges vary by laboratory; MedlinePlus lists 3.0 to 7.1 mg/dL for women and 4.0 to 8.6 mg/dL for men. For gout, the number that matters most is the saturation point of about 6.8 mg/dL, above which urate crystals can form. Definitions of hyperuricemia vary; the 2020 ACR guideline uses 6.8 mg/dL or higher. In the Normative Aging Study of men, annual gout incidence was 0.1 percent with urate below 7.0 mg/dL and 4.9 percent at 9 mg/dL or above. For people on urate-lowering therapy, the 2020 ACR target is a urate below 6 mg/dL; the guideline does not set a lower target for tophaceous gout. A normal reading during a flare does not rule out gout, and a high reading alone does not diagnose it.

gout-vs-pseudogout-guide.question: What is the difference between gout and pseudogout?
gout-vs-pseudogout-guide.answerHtml: Both cause sudden, painful joint swelling, hence the shared name, but they are caused by different crystals. Gout comes from monosodium urate crystals that form when urate builds up, often first hitting a big toe, and is treated long-term with urate-lowering drugs, with allopurinol preferred first-line per the 2020 ACR gout guideline. Pseudogout, properly called calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease, comes from calcium pyrophosphate crystals that form in cartilage, most often strikes the knee and then the wrist, is rare before age 60, and has no urate-lowering or disease-modifying drug. Instead, pseudogout flare treatment is anti-inflammatory (a steroid injected into the joint, colchicine, an NSAID, or an oral steroid; see the EULAR recommendations), and associated conditions such as hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, and low magnesium are screened for. The only way to tell them apart with certainty is to examine joint fluid and identify the crystal type.

canker-sore-treatment-guide.question: What is the best treatment for a canker sore in 2026?
canker-sore-treatment-guide.answerHtml: For most canker sores, a topical corticosteroid is the first-line treatment: it reduces pain and shortens healing time, per the StatPearls review of recurrent aphthous stomatitis and the 2026 umbrella review by Al-Aizari and colleagues. Generic triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% dental paste is labeled to be pressed onto the sore at bedtime and, if needed, two or three times a day after meals. Over-the-counter numbing gels ease pain, and in a systematic review of small crossover trials, a sodium lauryl sulfate-free toothpaste reduced the number, duration and pain of ulcers. Most canker sores heal on their own in 1 to 2 weeks. See a licensed clinician if an ulcer is larger than 1 cm, has lasted more than two weeks, keeps coming back, or comes with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, eye or genital ulcers, or a rash.

hives-treatment-guide.question: What is the first treatment for acute hives in adults?
hives-treatment-guide.answerHtml: For uncomplicated acute hives in adults, a standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamine is the usual first treatment, according to the 2026 international urticaria guideline. Cetirizine and fexofenadine are examples; use the product label and ask a clinician before increasing doses or combining medicines. An individual wheal usually fades within 24 hours, although new ones may appear, according to the AAAAI; recurring hives beyond 6 weeks need a chronic-urticaria evaluation. Hives with trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, faintness, or repeated vomiting can signal anaphylaxis: use prescribed epinephrine and call 911. Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine.

food-poisoning-treatment-guide.question: What are the first priorities in adult food poisoning treatment?
food-poisoning-treatment-guide.answerHtml: For an adult with mild, uncomplicated food poisoning, focus on three priorities: replace fluids, watch for warning signs, and choose medicines cautiously. IDSA guidance recommends oral rehydration solution for mild-to-moderate dehydration; severe dehydration or inability to drink needs in-person care. Antibiotics are not routine, and diarrhea medicines are unsafe in some infections. Norovirus usually improves in 1 to 3 days, but other causes can last longer. Bloody stools, high fever, repeated vomiting that prevents drinking, or very little urine warrant prompt assessment. For suspected norovirus, avoid preparing food for others until at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.

affordability/why-insured-cannot-afford-.question: Why do insured patients still struggle to afford care?
affordability/why-insured-cannot-afford-.answerHtml: Having health insurance in the United States no longer means health care is affordable. In KFF polling compiled in a brief updated October 23, 2026, 44% of adults said health care costs are difficult to afford (May 2025 poll), and 28% said they had skipped or postponed care they needed in the past 12 months because of cost (May 2026 survey) (KFF). The problem is no longer framed correctly when we talk only about the uninsured. The sharper story is about the insured.

affordability/what-is-coinsurance.question: What is coinsurance and how does it work with your deductible?
affordability/what-is-coinsurance.answerHtml: Coinsurance is the percentage you pay for a covered health care service after you have met your deductible. If your plan says "20% coinsurance," you pay 20% of the allowed amount and your plan pays 80%, but only after you have satisfied your deductible. Before that, you pay the full allowed amount yourself.

affordability/copay-vs-coinsurance-vs-de.question: What is the difference between a copay, coinsurance, and deductible?
affordability/copay-vs-coinsurance-vs-de.answerHtml: A copay is a flat dollar amount per service. Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost per service. A deductible is the amount you pay out of pocket before your plan starts paying for most services. They hit you in a specific order, and understanding that order is the key to predicting what any given visit or treatment will actually cost you.

affordability/out-of-pocket-maximum.question: What is an out-of-pocket maximum and how is it different from a deductible?
affordability/out-of-pocket-maximum.answerHtml: An out-of-pocket maximum is the most you have to pay out of your own money for covered, in-network care in a plan year. Once your deductibles, copays, and coinsurance add up to that number, your health plan pays 100% of your covered benefits for the rest of the year. It is the financial safety net built into every Affordable Care Act-compliant plan.

affordability/what-is-an-eob.question: What is an explanation of benefits (EOB) and how do you read it?
affordability/what-is-an-eob.answerHtml: An explanation of benefits, or EOB, is a document your health insurance company sends after it processes a claim for your care. It shows what your provider charged, what your plan is willing to pay, and what you are responsible for. The single most important thing to understand is that an EOB is not a bill, per CMS. It is a statement of how your insurer handled the claim. The bill comes separately from your provider.

affordability/what-care-costs-without-in.question: What does care cost without insurance?
affordability/what-care-costs-without-in.answerHtml: Without insurance, a routine primary care visit in the United States can cost roughly $40 to $300, and an urgent care visit roughly $125 to $300, according to consumer cost guides. These are wide ranges because the price depends on where you go, what you need, and whether you are quoted a cash price or a hospital list price. The most important thing to know is that the price is not fixed, and you can often look it up, or ask for a written estimate, before you go.

affordability/does-medical-debt-affect-c.question: Does medical debt affect your credit?
affordability/does-medical-debt-affect-c.answerHtml: Yes, medical debt can still affect your credit, but far less than it once did, and the rules have changed several times in the last few years. As of October 2026, there is no federal ban on medical debt appearing in credit reports, because the rule that would have created one was thrown out in court. What protects most people now is a set of voluntary policies from the three major credit bureaus, which keep three categories of medical debt off credit reports, plus laws in some states.

affordability/hospital-financial-assista.question: What is hospital financial assistance and charity care, and how do you apply?
affordability/hospital-financial-assista.answerHtml: Hospital financial assistance, often called charity care, is free or discounted care for people who cannot afford to pay. If you are facing a hospital bill you cannot cover, this is one of the first things to check, because federal law requires nonprofit hospitals to have a written financial assistance policy. Eligibility varies by hospital, so it is worth checking even if you have insurance.

affordability/what-to-do-when-you-cannot.question: What should you do when you cannot pay a medical bill?
affordability/what-to-do-when-you-cannot.answerHtml: A medical bill you cannot afford is not the end of the conversation. It is the start of a process that, done in order, can lead to a smaller amount, a payment plan, or in some cases no bill at all. The steps below draw mainly on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's guidance and apply whether or not you have insurance.

affordability/surprise-medical-bills.question: What are your rights under the No Surprises Act for a surprise medical bill?
affordability/surprise-medical-bills.answerHtml: CMS calls an unexpected balance bill from an out-of-network provider a surprise medical bill: the provider bills you for the difference between its charge and what your health plan paid. Starting in 2022, the No Surprises Act bans the most common types of these bills for people with private health insurance, and people who are uninsured or self-pay can often get a good faith estimate before care (CMS).

full-time-rv-living-health-guide.question: How do full-time RVers get health care and prescriptions on the road?
full-time-rv-living-health-guide.answerHtml: Living full time in an RV does not have to mean going without a doctor. The two problems that actually trip people up are prescription continuity across state lines and finding a clinician who can treat you when you have no fixed home address. Both are solvable with planning. Keep medications in their original bottles, carry a current list, and use a mail-order pharmacy tied to your state of residence so refills follow you instead of you chasing them. For new or urgent problems, a synchronous telehealth visit can manage most common on-the-road conditions, including uncomplicated urinary tract infections, seasonal allergies, sinus infections, rashes, tick bites, and traveler's diarrhea. Clinicians must be licensed or legally permitted to practice in the state where the patient is located, so telehealth works when the clinician is licensed where you are physically located at the time of the visit. Some conditions always need in-person care: chest pain, difficulty breathing, a fever with stiff neck, or a wound that needs stitches. Your single most important task is to establish one stable state of residence, because that state determines your Marketplace or Medicaid coverage, while which clinicians can treat you by telehealth depends on where you are at the time of the visit.

oral-thrush-treatment-guide.question: What is the usual 7 to 14 day treatment plan for oral thrush in adults?
oral-thrush-treatment-guide.answerHtml: For confirmed, uncomplicated oral thrush in adults, IDSA guidance recommends local antifungals for mild disease and fluconazole for moderate-to-severe disease, commonly for 7 to 14 days. Product directions matter: the clotrimazole label specifies 14 days, while the fluconazole label specifies at least 2 weeks. Do not copy a single-dose vaginal-yeast regimen or substitute skin cream. Confirm the diagnosis, check medicine interactions, and address triggers such as steroid inhalers or dentures. Painful or difficult swallowing, persistent disease, or repeated episodes require further assessment, not automatic repeat prescriptions.

insect-sting-reaction-guide.question: How do you treat a bee or wasp sting in the first 48 hours?
insect-sting-reaction-guide.answerHtml: A bee or wasp sting has 3 main reaction patterns: a small local reaction, a large local reaction, or a systemic allergic reaction. For symptoms confined to the sting area, remove a visible stinger promptly, wash the skin, and use a cloth-wrapped cold pack. Large local swelling may increase for 24 to 48 hours and usually subsides over 3 to 10 days; swelling alone does not prove infection. Trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, faintness, or rapidly developing symptoms away from the sting require emergency action. Use your prescribed epinephrine according to your action plan and call 911; do not wait for a video visit or an antihistamine. See the US stinging-insect practice parameter, CDC first aid, and World Allergy Organization emergency guidance.

sick-visiting-new-york-city-guide.question: How can a visitor get medical care while sick in New York City?
sick-visiting-new-york-city-guide.answerHtml: New York City drew 65 million visitors in 2025, including 12.5 million from outside the US (NYC Tourism + Conventions, March 2026). For a possible emergency, call 911: under the federal EMTALA law, Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency services must provide a medical screening exam and stabilizing treatment regardless of ability to pay, and the city's 11 public hospitals are run by NYC Health + Hospitals, which provides care regardless of ability to pay (NYC311). For non-emergencies, visitors can use urgent care centers, NYC Health + Hospitals ExpressCare, pharmacies, hotel-arranged house calls or telehealth. A prescription written at home cannot be filled in New York: pharmacies dispense only on a prescription from a person legally authorized to issue it (NY Education Law §6810), and New York prescriptions are sent electronically (NY Public Health Law §281). A US-licensed clinician who evaluates the visitor while they are physically in New York can decide whether a new prescription is appropriate and send it to a New York pharmacy.

malaria-prevention-pills-guide.question: How do adult travelers choose and time malaria prevention pills?
malaria-prevention-pills-guide.answerHtml: The right malaria pill depends on the destination's drug resistance, trip length, side effects, pregnancy and other medicines. Atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline start 1 to 2 days before travel, mefloquine at least 2 weeks before, and every regimen continues after you leave. Primaquine and tafenoquine need a G6PD blood test first. No pill is 100% effective, so a fever during or after travel needs prompt care and a malaria test.[1][2][4]

pre-travel-medical-visit-guide.question: What does a pre-travel medical visit cover, and which typhoid vaccine fits?
pre-travel-medical-visit-guide.answerHtml: A pre-travel visit reviews your health and itinerary and plans vaccines, medicines and prevention advice; CDC advises booking at least 4 to 6 weeks before departure, though it is never too late. Typhoid vaccine is recommended for travel to areas with recognized risk, highest in South Asia. The oral vaccine is 4 capsules every other day, finished at least 1 week before exposure; the shot is one injection at least 2 weeks before travel. Both protect 50% to 80% of people.[4][3][2]

stomach-flu-norovirus-guide.question: How long does the stomach flu last, and how is it treated?
stomach-flu-norovirus-guide.answerHtml: Norovirus, the most common cause of the stomach flu, usually starts 12 to 48 hours after exposure, and most people get better within 1 to 3 days.[1][4] There is no specific medicine and antibiotics do not help.[1] Oral rehydration solution is the first-line treatment for mild to moderate dehydration.[6] CDC advises staying home, and not preparing food or caring for others, until 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.[1][3] Signs of dehydration, a high fever, severe belly pain, or bloody or black stools need prompt medical care.[4]
